stocks.investment_implication: Trane Technologies’ Wide-Narrow moat (7.3) rests on pricing power and customer switching costs, and its widening trend points to a durable advantage. Approximate ROIC of 25.9%, consistently positive free cash flow and an operating margin that rose from 15.1% in 2022 to 18.6% in 2025 support the rating.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Trane attributed its 2024 gross margin expansion partly to price realization, showing an ability to capture value from its products and services.
stocks.key_risk: A more aggressive pricing cycle among HVAC competitors could weaken Trane’s pricing power and erode margins.

evidence: Trane Technologies’ operating margin increased from 15.1% (FY2022) to 16.4% (FY2023), 17.6% (FY2024), and 18.6% (FY2025), indicating improving profitability through recent cycles.

Trane Technologies’ free cash flow margin rose from 7.6% (FY2022) to 11.8% (FY2023) and peaked at 14.0% (FY2024), remaining high at 13.2% (FY2025), consistent with sustained value capture rather than margin leakage.

Trane Technologies reported gross profit margin expansion to 35.7% for the year ended December 31, 2024 (up 260 bps vs. 33.1% in 2023), attributing the increase primarily to gross productivity and price realization (partially offset by inflation).

Trane Technologies reported segment adjusted EBITDA margin expansion in 2024 that it attributed to price realization (e.g., segment adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.9% in 2024 vs. 19.3% in 2023, with the increase attributed primarily to price realization and gross productivity).

Trane Technologies’ ROIC was approximately 23.5% in the latest year shown, which supports that the company is sustaining returns likely associated with differentiation and/or pricing power rather than competing as a pure price-taker.
risks: Direct brand-loyalty metrics (e.g., NPS, retention/churn rates, customer survey scores) and explicit “premium vs. competitors” pricing quantification are not clearly evidenced in the available filings/sources used here, limiting confidence in the Brand Loyalty component.

HVAC-equipment demand is cyclical and can be affected by construction cycles, which may pressure pricing/volume even if the brand is strong; profitability momentum could weaken if volumes fall and competitive pricing intensifies.

evidence: Trane Technologies reported $347.6 million of research and development spend in 2025 (10-K), with R&D focused on product/system sustainability improvements and lower global warming potential refrigerants—supporting an ongoing IP/technology-development flywheel rather than a one-off advantage.

Trane Technologies’ scale and manufacturing footprint are hard to replicate quickly: as of Dec. 31, 2025 it owned/leased ~31 million sq. ft. worldwide, with manufacturing/assembly primarily conducted in 38 plants.
Capital expenditure required to maintain/expand capacity is substantial: total capital expenditures were $383.0 million in 2025 and $370.6 million in 2024 (10-K).

Trane Technologies reports strength in refrigerant/HVACR technology protection and compliance in the U.S.: a U.S. DOE document states Trane has over 500 active U.S. patents and annual U.S. HVACR sales of more than $8 billion (supports meaningful, sustained technical/IP presence).

Regulatory-compliance barriers exist in refrigerants and equipment approvals: EPA SNAP rules include product use conditions tied to safety standards (e.g., UL 60335-2-40 Edition 3) for certain lower-flammability refrigerants; entrants must therefore navigate product approval/standards compliance to compete in compliant HVACR offerings.
risks: Patent-specific metrics (e.g., exact global active patent count, top patent families, and a quantified expiry/overhang schedule) could not be verified from high-quality primary disclosures in the available evidence set, limiting the confidence in how durable the patent moat is over the next decade.

Trane itself states it does not consider any single patent or proprietary technology as material to the overall business, which can indicate the moat is distributed across many technologies rather than dominated by a single protected asset (reducing the certainty that barriers are near-impenetrable).

Competing HVAC/building-equipment manufacturers (e.g., other global HVAC OEMs) can still launch competing products without needing to match Trane’s entire manufacturing footprint immediately, making competition more likely to focus on specific product lines rather than forcing full parity across the portfolio.

evidence: Trane reports that its service and maintenance contracts (preventative/repair agreements) have a typical length of 12 to 60 months, creating multi-year customer commitment and reducing near-term churn incentives.

Trane sells extended warranties that can last up to five years, with revenue recognized over the life of the contract; these multi-year coverage periods further extend the time horizon during which customers may be economically reluctant to switch away from Trane-supported service.

Trane’s connected services terms explicitly grant Trane rights to access/monitor/control customers’ connected equipment and to view/collect/extract/transmit/process/use “System Data,” and covers cloud software and remote monitoring delivered under subscription-like connected mechanical/building services agreements—supporting ecosystem lock-in via ongoing data/remote diagnostics.

A Trane commercial HVAC sales document claims that when customers want to handle existing systems, the commonly cited alternative approach is a “rip & replace” solution that “often times can cost 3-4X more” than a Trane bridge-based communications approach—implying high migration cost/time friction when switching building automation/control components.

A report cited by Facilities Dive states Trane’s proprietary diagnostic software creates “knowledge barriers” so third-party service providers “cannot access system data,” and it highlights a 92% service contract renewal rate—direct evidence consistent with high renewal stickiness (and therefore switching friction).
risks: The 92% service contract renewal figure is sourced from a third-party report rather than directly from Trane’s audited filings, so the exact magnitude for all segments/geographies may be overstated or differ from Trane’s reported renewal metrics.

While Trane documents multi-year service/extended-warranty terms and data-access rights, publicly available sources do not provide a quantified, customer-specific migration cost (e.g., average $ or months to switch off Tracer/connected services) across a representative customer cohort.

evidence: Trane reported a growing connected base: it stated in 2024 that it supports “over 2 million pieces of connected equipment” and “~40,000 connected buildings.”

Trane indicated rapid reinforcement of its connected installed base in 2025, stating it has “over 65,000 connected buildings,” adding “about a building an hour on average,” implying a significant ongoing net inflow of connected assets.

Trane described monetizable, contract-like engagement tied to installed connected systems, stating that its service model has evolved from break/fix toward being “connected to the asset” for performance/energy monitoring and remote support.

Trane’s financials show strong and improving operating profitability alongside revenue growth (revenue: $16.0B in 2022 to $21.3B in 2025; operating margin: 15.1% to 18.6%; net margin: 11.0% to 13.7%), consistent with an installed-base/services strategy that can benefit from higher network-value per customer over time.

Connected-services contractual ability for recurring monitoring/control/data use exists in Trane’s customer terms, granting access to monitor/control connected systems and enabling subscribed cloud services (Connected Services terms list multiple cloud/SaaS offerings under subscription agreements).
risks: Connected-assets network effects may be less defensible than typical two-sided marketplaces because Trane’s “network” is primarily an installed equipment/services layer in HVAC, not a buyer–seller platform with liquidity and switching costs that scale via third-party participation.

Competitors with large installed bases (e.g., other HVAC OEMs and building automation providers) can replicate connected monitoring and service offerings, limiting winner-take-most dynamics even if Trane’s connected base is large.

evidence: Trane Technologies grew revenue from $16.0B (2022) to $21.3B (2025) while expanding operating margin from 15.1% to 18.6% (and net margin from 11.0% to 13.7%), indicating scale-driven operating leverage rather than purely pricing cycles.

Cost per unit signal via gross productivity: in the 2024 Form 10-K discussion, Trane reported gross profit margin increased to 35.7% in 2024 (vs 33.1% in 2023) driven primarily by “gross productivity and price realization,” with inflation partially offsetting; this is consistent with scalable unit-cost takeouts.

Supply-chain / volume-throughput benefit: Trane attributed margin expansion in 2024 to “gross productivity and higher volumes,” with “adjusted EBITDA margin” increasing by 160 bps to 20.9% in 2024 vs 19.3% in 2023; this suggests scale is translating into better factory economics rather than only SG&A discipline.

Economies-of-scale + overhead absorption: Selling & administrative expense as a % of net revenues increased from 16.7% to 18.1% in 2024 (so SG&A is not the main driver), while operating margin still rose to 18.6% by 2025; combined with high ROIC (~23.5% latest year) this supports that scale benefits show up more in manufacturing/productivity and gross margin than in SG&A leverage.

Scale is large enough to compete effectively globally with structural product/process advantages: 2024 segment adjusted EBITDA margin increased to 20.9% (from 19.3%), and 2024 commentary explicitly ties margin improvement to “gross productivity” and “higher volumes,” implying competitors must match both throughput and productivity to stay cost-competitive.
risks: The clearest “unit cost” evidence found is embedded in qualitative disclosures (e.g., “gross productivity”) rather than a direct published metric like cost per unit by product line, so the economies-of-scale claim is partially inferential from margins.

HVAC/building-equipment margins can be influenced by pricing realization, mix, and industry cycle; if cost productivity gains slow, margin expansion could become less persistent even if scale remains.

bear_case: Trane’s own Connected Services terms reserve broad rights for Trane to modify, update, discontinue, deprecate, or remove Connected Services features and integrations, which weakens the durability of any “network effect” or ecosystem lock-in argument based on stable functionality.

Trane Connected Services allow Trane to access/monitor/control the customer’s equipment and to view/collect/extract/process “System Data,” but the Facilities Dive report claims Trane’s diagnostic software creates “knowledge barriers” such that third-party service providers cannot access system data, which implies the ecosystem may be vulnerable to regulatory or procurement pushback if customers seek data portability.

There is litigation-related evidence in HVAC industry filings and complaints that market shares can be sticky and may not shift much (“shares don’t shift a lot”), but that same evidence suggests the competitive model is more about incremental price/placement discipline than strong differentiation translating into sustained share gains—leaving the moat vulnerable to a future re-pricing cycle if competitors choose to compete harder.

stocks.investment_implication: Union Pacific’s stable Wide-Narrow moat rests on economies of scale and the high cost of replicating its rail network. Its 15.8% return on invested capital, consistently high operating margins and positive free cash flow support the moat’s durability, though competition limits its reach.
stocks.key_strength: Economies of Scale: Union Pacific’s extensive network supports efficient operations, with a 40.2% operating margin and 22.4% free cash flow margin in 2025.
stocks.key_risk: Competition from BNSF and other transport providers threatens Union Pacific’s traffic and pricing power, particularly as intermodal volumes weaken.

evidence: Union Pacific sustained very high profitability over 2022–2025 with operating margin of 39.9% (2022), 37.7% (2023), 40.1% (2024), and 40.2% (2025), indicating stable-to-strong ability to hold pricing/mix despite demand volatility.

Net margin remained elevated and resilient at 28.1% (2022), 26.4% (2023), 27.8% (2024), and 29.1% (2025), supporting that pricing power (and/or cost pass-through) has not structurally eroded over the last few years.

Union Pacific’s freight pricing and revenue management are evidenced in its disclosures that freight revenue changes are driven by 'core pricing gains' plus fuel surcharges; for 2023, freight revenues were down 3% year-over-year to $22.6B but 'partially offset by core pricing gains,' and UP separately reports fuel surcharge programs generating $3.0B (2023) and $3.7B (2022).

Customer value/relationship strength signals for brand-like loyalty are supported by UP’s intermodal customer service survey results: in the latest survey covering the second half of 2025, UP received 'good' or 'very good' ratings from 80% of respondents.

Premium/price differentiation appears to persist in UP’s own business mix: UP reports that in 2024, 'Premium' shipments generated 31% of total freight revenues, aligning with a higher-value service tier where customers are more likely to accept pricing for service reliability and routing options.
risks: UP’s apparent pricing power is partially intertwined with fuel surcharge mechanisms; fuel surcharge revenues varied with diesel prices (e.g., $3.7B in 2022 vs $3.0B in 2023), so margin resilience may not purely reflect discretionary brand-driven pricing power.

Rail service reliability/operational disruptions can weaken customer willingness to pay (e.g., customer complaints and regulator scrutiny in prior periods indicate service performance can become a constraint on upselling or retention).

Unlike consumer or software brands, 'brand loyalty' in rail freight can be constrained by contractual tendering and limited modal substitution, so measured loyalty may be better explained by network/service performance than by a durable consumer-style brand.

evidence: Union Pacific operates a rail network of 32,889 route miles across the western two-thirds of the U.S., which materially raises the scale and right-of-way footprint an entrant would need to replicate to compete meaningfully. (Source: Union Pacific 2025 Form 10-K.)

Union Pacific has spent approximately $2.9 billion to deploy Positive Train Control (PTC), and completed installation on its required 17,000 miles by September 2018—creating a multi-year, FRA-regulated technology/engineering effort that a new entrant would need to fund and implement to operate at comparable safety/compliance levels. (Source: UP PTC implementation announcement.)

Union Pacific’s disclosed capital plan indicates sustained high reinvestment needs: in 2025 it expected a capital plan of approximately $3.4 billion (consistent with 2024), and 2024 capital expenditures were $3.452 billion. A well-funded entrant still must match this level of network and equipment reinvestment to sustain service levels. (Source: UP 2024/2025 disclosure.)

Union Pacific’s PTC implementation is explicitly tied to regulatory process (submitting a PTC Safety Plan to obtain PTC requirements coverage), implying regulatory/compliance steps that are not easily shortcut by an entrant without equivalent FRA interaction and system engineering. (Source: FRA/UP PTC documentation referencing PTCSP submission.)

Union Pacific’s technology base includes multiple safety/operations systems that would be costly and time-consuming for a new operator to replicate, including PTC and Energy Management Systems (EMS) that operate in conjunction with PTC; UP has also reported operating EMS on a large portion of its locomotive fleet since PTC rollout. (Sources: UP EMS/PTC and technology pages.)
risks: Patent-based defensibility appears weak for this moat dimension based on available evidence (public third-party patent-count summaries are low/unclear), so if regulation/scale are less defensible than assumed, the barrier score could be overstated.

Railroading remains competitive without a legal exclusivity franchise in the way a utility might have; an entrant can theoretically form service via trackage rights, leasing, or acquisition (though often at reduced competitiveness), which can cap the practical level of barrier even if replication is expensive. (Source: UP’s 10-K discussion of competition from other railroads and motor carriers.)

Network expansion or service build-outs take time and depend on rights-of-way availability, labor, and safety performance; if these constraints loosen (e.g., through acquisitions or regulatory changes), entry barriers may weaken. (Source context: UP’s ongoing compliance/safety environment and FRA oversight topics.)

evidence: Union Pacific’s 2024 SEC filing states its freight revenues are derived from contracts with customers for transportation from origin to destination, with each freight shipment generally treated as a distinct performance obligation (commitment starts with tendering/acceptance of the freight bill of lading and is satisfied upon delivery).

Union Pacific’s 2024 SEC filing indicates “customer incentives” are primarily provided for shipping to/from specific locations or based on cumulative volumes and are accounted for as reductions to operating revenues, suggesting incentives tied to volume rather than clearly documented, proprietary data/integration lock-in that would make migration technically difficult.

Union Pacific’s contract accounting discloses that under typical payment terms customers pay after each performance obligation is satisfied and that there are no material contract assets or liabilities associated with freight revenues (i.e., the rail service is not described as a customer-held prepay/minimum-commitment structure that would typically increase migration penalties).

Union Pacific discloses customer churn metrics are not provided in its 2024 10-K, and the filing does not describe customer retention/renewal rates, multi-year termination penalties, or switching/migration costs; instead it emphasizes ongoing competition for price, transit time, and quality/reliability.

Union Pacific explicitly discloses that it faces competition from other railroads and other transportation providers (motor carriers, ships, barges, pipelines) with competition also related to transit times and service reliability—implying customers can re-route/divert to alternatives when economics/service change, which constrains how high switching costs can be for customers.
risks: The 10-K does not provide explicit figures on minimum commitments, termination fees, or contract durations for shippers, so the switching-cost score may be understated if major private rate/volume agreements impose meaningful penalties that are not disclosed in the filing.

The rail industry can create operational switching friction (network fit, interchange/local facility constraints, routing, and equipment logistics) that may not appear as proprietary lock-in in SEC disclosures; without shipment-by-shipment diversion evidence, migration cost may be partially unobserved.

evidence: Union Pacific’s reported freight volumes show no sustained growth in the last 3 years: total revenue carloads were 8.0 million (2021), 8.169 million (2022), and 8.112 million (2023) with 2023 down ~1% vs. 2022, and intermodal revenue carloads were 3.211 million (2021), 3.116 million (2022), and 3.028 million (2023) with 2023 down ~3% vs. 2022. (These are company-reported figures in UP’s 2023 Form 10‑K).

Union Pacific’s intermodal revenue declined in 2023 versus 2022: intermodal freight revenues were $4.554B (2023) vs. $5.160B (2022), a ~12% decrease, indicating that any ‘more users → more value’ dynamic is not showing up as growth reinforcement in the core interchange/intermodal franchise over that period.

Union Pacific’s operating performance (a proxy for competitive advantage) is strong but does not clearly evidence accelerating network effects: operating margin was 39.9% (2022), 37.7% (2023), 40.1% (2024), and 40.2% (2025), with ROIC ~14.9% in the latest year shown by the user. High margins in a capital-intensive network can reflect cost/asset advantages rather than measurable cross-side network effects.

UP explicitly frames its network value more as service coverage/route advantages than as a marketplace with self-reinforcing liquidity: UP states it has the largest intermodal network in North America (service/footprint claim) and that it “added nearly one million in incremental lift capacity since 2021,” which supports capacity-driven competitiveness, not a clear, measurable network-effect flywheel (buyers attracting more sellers/users).

Competition/alternative networks remain material rather than weakening: UP references that in markets where UP competes head-to-head, BNSF already has 53% of the business and holds 60% of the intermodal market (UP’s own merger-related messaging), which is inconsistent with a ‘winner-take-most network’ narrative strengthening over time.
risks: Railroads are not classic digital marketplaces; network effects may be expressed more through fixed infrastructure density, schedules, and service performance than via measurable ‘users’ and cross-side liquidity metrics, so the absence of explicit user-count growth may understate underlying network externalities.

The evidence base gathered here relies on company-reported volume/revenue carload trends (carloads and intermodal revenue carloads) but does not include complete 3–5 year participation metrics (e.g., number of shipper contracts, active intermodal lanes/participants, or explicit marketplace liquidity), so the network-effects score could be understated.

evidence: Union Pacific generated very large operating margins of 39.9% (2022), 37.7% (2023), 40.1% (2024), and 40.2% (2025) while revenue was roughly flat at $24.875B (2022), $24.119B (2023), $24.250B (2024), and $24.510B (2025), consistent with a cost structure that is not easily matched by smaller rail operators.

Operating leverage at the business-model level is evident in the operating margin staying near ~38–40% despite only -0.5% revenue CAGR; this implies costs scale at least as fast as demand (or can be controlled) rather than rising one-for-one with revenue (revenue grew slowly, margins remained high).

Union Pacific reports fuel-consumption improvements that reduce unit operating input intensity (fuel consumption rate of 1.088 in 2023 vs 1.082 in 2024) alongside scale-driven throughput metrics (2024 vs 2023 fuel consumption rate down while gross ton-miles increased ~1% year-over-year), indicating network efficiency improvements that support lower unit costs at volume.

Union Pacific’s network productivity metrics improved in 2025 (freight car velocity 239 daily miles per car in 2025 vs 219 in 2024; locomotive productivity 141 GTMs per horsepower day in 2025 vs 136 in 2024), which typically lowers cost per car-mile/ton-mile by spreading fixed network costs over more productive capacity.

Scale shows up as sustained cash generation: free cash flow margin of 23.1% (2022), 19.8% (2023), 24.3% (2024), and 22.4% (2025), while operating margin remained ~38–40%—supporting that cost leadership is not just accounting margin but also converts into substantial cash.
risks: Rails are a structurally high-fixed-cost business, but not every cost component is purely scale-driven; labor/inflation, service mix, and one-time items can overwhelm any scale advantage in certain years.

Evidence for direct 'unit cost per mile' dominance versus each smaller competitor is not fully pinned down here (e.g., no comprehensive per-car-mile or per-ton-mile cost disclosure for all peers), so the economies-of-scale score relies on operating-margin/cash-flow and operating-performance metric improvements as proxies.

bear_case: Union Pacific’s own operating revenue disclosures show pricing strength is not “pure” discretionary pricing: 2024 operating revenue was up while operating revenue drivers included “core pricing gains,” but also “reduced fuel surcharge revenue,” and 2025 results cited “reduced fuel surcharge revenue” as a partially offsetting factor.

Intermodal competitiveness is showing demand/traffic softness rather than strengthening network advantage: Union Pacific disclosed intermodal revenue carloads fell year-over-year (e.g., 2025 intermodal units down vs. 2024, with intermodal units/revenue also cited as down in 2025 results materials).

Customer switching risk remains real and evidenced by regulatory exposure over pricing/charges: the Surface Transportation Board issued a decision partially granting complaints regarding Union Pacific’s charges tied to empty, privately owned tank cars moving to repair facilities—indicating shippers can successfully challenge UP’s charge practices rather than being insulated by lock-in.

Head-to-head share remains dominated by the larger rival rather than implying a compounding network flywheel for UP: UP stated that where it competes directly with BNSF, BNSF already has 53% of the business and holds 60% of the intermodal market.

stocks.investment_implication: Johnson Controls’ narrow moat rests on technical barriers to entry and some pricing power in its building products and services. Its 14.2% return on invested capital, consistently positive operating margins and free cash flow support the rating. The moat looks durable but stable, with competition limiting its strength.
stocks.key_strength: High Barriers to Entry: Johnson Controls’ patents and building-technology expertise make its products and systems harder for new entrants to replicate.
stocks.key_risk: Competition from established alternatives such as Honeywell, Siemens and Schneider Electric could limit Johnson Controls’ pricing power.

evidence: Johnson Controls reported operating margin of 10.8% (FY2023) and 10.5% (FY2024), rising to 12.0% (FY2025) and 15.6% (FY2026), indicating improved profitability over the last ~3 years.

Gross profit dollars and gross margin expanded: FY2024 gross margin was 35.2% and FY2025 gross margin increased to 36.4%, with the company attributing the gross profit increase to 'margin improvements in Products and Systems' plus higher volumes for Products and Systems and Services.

Pricing pass-through and resilience are explicitly discussed in relation to tariff-related cost pressure: Johnson Controls said it was passing along some price increases 'one for one' to customers (and cited tariff exposure of ~2% of sales or ~3% of cost of goods sold), consistent with some ability to protect pricing rather than being fully price-taker.

Customer-relationship economics are supported by service/installed-base framing in earnings materials: Johnson Controls described service growth as building on its 'installed base' and noted contract/attrition dynamics as a key variable that management monitors, which is directionally consistent with repeat business in services rather than purely commodity re-sales.

Portfolio mix supports monetization of differentiated offerings: in fiscal 2025, products and systems were ~68% of continuing-operations sales and services ~32% (services typically being the lever for recurring revenue and repeat contracts).
risks: The company’s disclosed contract-competition factors include 'quality, price, design, reputation, technology' and many large competitors across HVAC/controls/fire/security, so differentiation may not translate into a stable, measurable price premium across all categories.

No direct, company-specific public metric was found here for brand loyalty (e.g., NPS, retention/renewal rates, churn/installed-base retention) or for the magnitude of price premium versus key competitors (e.g., YORK/Metasys pricing vs Carrier/Trane/Schneider).

evidence: Johnson Controls reported capital expenditures of $434 million in fiscal 2025, down from $494 million in fiscal 2024 and $446 million in fiscal 2023—indicating a sustained (but not rapidly rising) internal investment level that a new entrant would need to match to compete in similar building-technology products/services.

Johnson Controls’ patent footprint appears broad and durable: its publicly listed U.S. patent catalog includes multiple named technology lines (e.g., OpenBlue, Metasys, HVAC controls and actuators), and the list page states it was last revised on August 21, 2026, implying an actively maintained IP estate rather than a static legacy portfolio.

Johnson Controls disclosed in investor/earnings materials that it holds “over 270 patents” related to compressor technology and “over 220 patents” related to Variable Speed Drives (VSDs), which raises the cost of technical replication for entrants attempting to compete on these efficiency/performance components.

Johnson Controls indicated its technology platform is differentiated but competitive: the company’s fiscal 2025 annual report describes OpenBlue as combining its building expertise with AI/ML-powered services (e.g., remote diagnostics and predictive maintenance) and notes competition with large incumbents (Honeywell, Siemens, Schneider Electric, Carrier/Trane/others) plus a fragmented market—supporting that differentiation exists, but is not a single-company regulatory monopoly.

Johnson Controls’ own patent list shows continuing application in building controls/automation products (e.g., multiple controller and management-related patent entries displayed on the company-maintained page), consistent with an IP barrier that can help defend installed-base integrations and control logic against copycat offerings.
risks: The evidence gathered does not provide a clear, company-specific patent expiry/remaining-life timeline for Johnson Controls’ most economically important patents; without expiry granularity, the durability of IP barriers over the next 10 years is harder to quantify.

Building automation and control markets are described as competitive and fragmented in the company’s filings and industry context; if core differentiation shifts toward quickly-mimicked platform integrations or if customers standardize on interoperability ecosystems, the effective barrier could weaken despite the patent portfolio.

evidence: Johnson Controls’ remaining performance obligations for large, long-lived construction/service contracts include average initial contract terms of 25 to 35 years for the entire contract (while backlog approximates a ~5-year lifecycle period), which implies structurally long customer commitments in segments where JCI is installed for decades.

Johnson Controls states that it enters into extended warranties and long-term service/maintenance agreements with certain customers, indicating service offerings that can create continuing obligations beyond initial installation.

JCI markets Metasys (a flagship building automation platform) as being used in more than 54,000 locations worldwide, and Metasys includes ongoing upgrade/integration capabilities; an installed base of this size increases the likelihood of switching friction for customers tied to Metasys operational tooling and configuration.

Johnson Controls highlights both ‘open’/standard protocol compatibility and migration/upgrade pathways (e.g., documentation noting that software/hardware portfolios can be upgraded/migrated using Johnson Controls upgrade mechanisms), suggesting switching is not purely proprietary lock-in but can still involve operational and project costs during upgrades/migrations.

Service-contract terms in filings indicate that some service contracts are one year or less and may be cancellable without substantial penalty, which limits the overall ‘always-on’ nature of switching costs across the whole customer base (i.e., not all relationships are necessarily hard to exit).
risks: Reliable, company-specific quantitative churn/retention metrics for JCI’s service contracts (e.g., contract attrition rates by segment) were not found in the sources gathered here; without those numbers, the switching-cost score relies on installed-base and contract-duration evidence rather than demonstrated customer exit behavior.

Metasys is described as compatible with standard building protocols and controllers from other manufacturers, which can reduce the practical cost of migration versus a fully proprietary stack; this could mean switching costs are lower than what the installed-base size alone would imply.

evidence: Johnson Controls positions its digital/data platform (OpenBlue) as enabling “data-driven ‘smart building’ services and solutions” that combine building products/services with cloud/on-premises software capabilities (predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics, workplace management, compliance monitoring, advanced risk assessments), but it does not disclose a measurable OpenBlue user/community size that grows with additional users (fiscal 2025 annual report).

The strongest identifiable ‘installed-base’ network dynamic is lifecycle attachment and recurring revenue: the company states it has a “large base of current customers” that leads to “significant repeat business for the maintenance, retrofit and replacement markets” and that it can “leverage its installed base to generate sales for its service business” (fiscal 2025 annual report).

Johnson Controls explicitly relies on a direct installation channel that “creates a large installed base of our fire and security solutions and HVAC equipment,” which in turn creates “opportunities for longer term service, monitoring, solutions and retrofit revenue,” but it frames this as channel/install-base linkage rather than a cross-party marketplace network (fiscal 2025 annual report risk factor).

The company reports recurring revenue contract types (e.g., Planned Service Agreement, O&M, facility management, building monitoring, subscriber contracts, subscription models, as-a-Service, leasing and monitoring) as recurring revenue, but it does not provide subscriber counts, monitored endpoints, or cross-side participation metrics that would directly evidence network effects strengthening with user growth (fiscal 2025 annual report).
risks: Direct/indirect network effects are not clearly measurable from disclosed metrics: the company does not provide OpenBlue active customer counts, monitored device/endpoint counts, or security monitoring subscriber numbers over 3–5 years that would demonstrate network-effect-driven acceleration.

Competing building-technology ecosystems (e.g., Honeywell, Siemens Smart Infrastructure, Schneider Electric, Carrier/Trane, Vertiv, plus fragmented regional players) suggest customers can standardize around multiple incumbents without a winner-take-most, two-sided liquidity dynamic (fiscal 2025 annual report competition section).

A meaningful portion of value appears to come from installed base + services attachment (switching costs and lifecycle contracts) rather than from network effects that increase in value as other participants join; this can weaken durability versus true platform/network dynamics.

evidence: Johnson Controls revenue scaled from $22.3B (FY2023) to $23.0B (FY2024) to $23.6B (FY2025) to $25.7B (FY2026), while operating margin expanded to 15.6% in FY2026 (vs. 10.8% in FY2023).

Operating leverage is evident in the cost structure: SG&A dollars rose from $5.764B (FY2025) to $5.510B (FY2026) while revenue rose to $25.666B (FY2026) from $23.596B (FY2025), consistent with scale improving overhead absorption.

Gross profit grew faster than revenue in FY2026 vs FY2025: gross profit increased to $9.515B (FY2026) from $8.592B (FY2025) on higher revenue of $25.666B (FY2026) vs $23.596B (FY2025), supporting a scale-driven unit economics improvement (at least in this period).

Scale appears to translate into cash generation durability: free cash flow margin increased to 12.9% in FY2026 (from 4.1% in FY2025), with FY2026 continuing-operations cash provided by operating activities of $3.872B (vs. $2.554B in FY2025).

Market-size evidence suggests meaningful scale/leadership in adjacent building controls markets: a building automation & control systems market estimate places Johnson Controls as the largest competitor with ~6.98% share (and cites top players including Honeywell, Siemens, ABB).
risks: The strongest margin/cash improvements coincide with a period that includes large items/discontinuities in the financials (e.g., discontinued operations and business divestitures), which can complicate isolating pure ongoing economies-of-scale from one-time mix/portfolio effects.

The building technologies/solutions space is described as fragmented with many competitors, limiting the extent to which any single firm’s scale can permanently force others out purely via lower unit cost.

bear_case: Johnson Controls disclosed Systems business margin pressure in China: in its Q2 FY2024 earnings release, segment EBITA margin declined versus the prior year, driven “primarily” by continued declines in the Systems business in China.

Johnson Controls’ free-cash-flow conversion deteriorated sharply after FY2025 despite revenue growth—free cash flow margin fell from 7.0% (FY2024) to 4.1% (FY2025), before only partially recovering to 12.9% in FY2026.

A recent U.S. Department of Justice settlement states Johnson Controls and two subsidiaries agreed to pay $5 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations tied to failing to comply with cybersecurity requirements in federal contracts and subcontracts for building products and services.

Johnson Controls’ competitive positioning does not imply a durable moat shield: market-facing commentary and competitive listings consistently place multiple large incumbents (e.g., Honeywell, Siemens, Schneider Electric, Carrier/Trane, ABB) as direct alternatives in building automation/control systems, reducing the likelihood of sustained category-level pricing power.

stocks.investment_implication: Constellation Brands has a stable, narrow moat rooted in brand loyalty and economies of scale. Approximate return on invested capital of 12.1%, consistently positive operating margins and free cash flow support the assessment, though declining beer shipments and rising costs limit its durability.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Modelo Especial’s leading U.S. beer sales demonstrate consumer preference that supports Constellation’s pricing power.
stocks.key_risk: Declining beer shipments and higher costs, including aluminum tariffs, could erode the profitability of Constellation’s brands.

evidence: Constellation Brands’ operating margin was 30.1% (FY2023), 32.0% (FY2024), 33.0% (FY2025), and 31.3% (FY2026), indicating sustained profitability through the last 3–4 fiscal years rather than a material erosion of brand-enabled economics.

Constellation Brands maintained strong free cash flow generation at 18.2% (FY2023), 15.2% (FY2024), 19.0% (FY2025), and 19.6% (FY2026), consistent with pricing/portfolio mix supporting cash economics even as revenue declined (9.5, 10.0, 10.2, 9.1 USD bn).

Constellation Brands’ pricing/brand contribution is evidenced by management’s stated expectation to realize ~1% to 2% of “pricing benefits” each year on average (i.e., pack size and innovation are part of the approach, but management explicitly models ongoing pricing capture).

In U.S. tracked beer channels, Constellation Brands reported brand strength and mix momentum via Circana share metrics: Modelo Especial was the #1 beer brand by dollar sales and a #1 dollar share gainer (reported for fiscal periods including FY2024 and continued into later updates), implying sustained consumer preference that supports category pricing power for its branded portfolio.

Constellation Brands’ gross margin has been stable around the ~50% area over multiple fiscal years (e.g., ~50.4% in FY2023 and FY2024, and ~52.1% in FY2025, with FY2026 ~51.6% shown in third-party compilations), indicating pricing/mix is not being competed away to commodity levels.
risks: Reported net margin swings sharply across the period (-0.8% in FY2023, 17.3% in FY2024, -0.8% in FY2025, 18.5% in FY2026), which can obscure underlying brand pricing power by introducing non-operating or one-time effects.

Revenue declined overall across FY2023–FY2026 (from 9.5 to 9.1 USD bn; CAGR ~-1.1%), suggesting pricing power may be offset at times by volume, mix, promotional intensity, or category contraction rather than expanding premium monetization.

evidence: Constellation reports large, ongoing beer-capacity spending: fiscal 2026 capital expenditures totaled $875.0 million, with $762.4 million related to the Beer segment, and management planned about $800 million for fiscal 2027 capex (almost entirely focused on Brewery Projects).

Constellation’s U.S. beer market position is underpinned by contractually exclusive, perpetual brand rights: the company states it has the exclusive right to import, market, and sell its beer brands in all 50 U.S. states, and it also states it owns the brand license for Corona and Modelo in the U.S. to import, market, and sell exclusively and perpetually.

Regulatory/compliance friction exists for any new entrant trying to sell or import beer into the U.S.: the U.S. Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) requires permits for persons who wholesale or import alcohol beverages and requires TTB label-bottle approval (COLA) for imported bottled beverage alcohol products.

Constellation indicates that beer capacity additions are not instantaneous: the fiscal 2026 10-K describes substantial “modular capacity addition activities” and “Brewery Projects,” including that initial production at the Veracruz Brewery is expected to commence around the middle of fiscal 2027 (implying multi-year build cycles for meaningful capacity parity).

Constellation’s own patent/IP signals appear limited relative to regulation/contract and capex barriers: public sources found quickly do not provide an authoritative, current patent-count and expiry timeline from Constellation filings (and a patent-history aggregator did not disclose a full portfolio without access), so patent strength is not evidenced as the primary entry barrier in the accessible materials.
risks: U.S. beer category competition is still viable through non-licensed brands: even with exclusive brand rights for Corona/Modelo, entrants can compete effectively by building alternative portfolios and distribution relationships, limiting how much exclusivity can block overall beer competition.

The TTB permit/label process is a barrier to entry, but it is typically not decades-long; a well-funded entrant may still establish U.S. import/marketing operations within a few years, so regulatory friction alone may not prevent competitive parity long term.

Evidence for patents/time-to-parity via proprietary technology is not strong in readily accessible sources; if Constellation’s moat relies more on brand licenses and capacity than on defensible brewing-process IP, barrier durability could be weaker than a patent-centric thesis.

evidence: Constellation Brands reports that net sales are highly concentrated in distributors: net sales to its 10 largest customers represented ~59% of net sales in FY2025 (year ended Feb 28, 2025) and ~58% in FY2024 (year ended Feb 29, 2024), indicating reliance on a small set of distribution counterparties rather than software/data lock-in.

Constellation Brands discloses that its arrangements with certain customers may generally be terminated by either party with prior notice, which implies no strong contractual termination penalties or long-term minimum commitments that would materially prevent switching away from Constellation.

Constellation Brands states it has an exclusive perpetual brand license to produce and market its Mexican beer portfolio in the U.S.; this brand/IP exclusivity is a constraint on other producers, but it is not a switching-cost mechanism imposed on Constellation’s customers (it does not make distributors/retailers unable to switch suppliers).

Constellation Brands’ customer payments are collected through independent distributors with predetermined collection dates arranged through electronic funds transfer, consistent with a standardized, transactional wholesale workflow rather than proprietary workflow systems that are costly to migrate away from.

Constellation Brands plans depletion/inventory reductions “with key distributors” following 2025 wine divestitures, evidencing that distributor relationships and volume allocations can be adjusted due to portfolio/inventory actions rather than being protected by heavy switching frictions or migration costs.
risks: The disclosures found do not provide customer churn/retention by distributor/channel, nor explicit migration time/cost estimates for switching Constellation’s brands to competitors; absence of evidence can understate switching costs.

Beer/wine/spirits distribution is capacity- and relationship-based, and Constellation may have trade spending, promotion, and allocation programs that can create commercial friction; however, specific quantified switching costs (e.g., contract durations, termination fees, minimum purchase obligations) were not located in the retrieved sources.

evidence: Constellation Brands’ revenue CAGR over the last four fiscal years (2023–2026) is approximately -1.1% (from $9.5B in FY2023 to $9.1B in FY2026), indicating no clear scaling in a broader “network” footprint over this period.

Constellation reports ongoing share gains and market leadership in beer (e.g., it states it has “Modelo Especial… the best-selling beer overall” and “#1 share gainer” leadership in the U.S. beer market/high-end segment), but these are brand and distribution execution advantages rather than explicit two-sided marketplace network effects.

Constellation’s FY2025 Beer performance attributes Beer net sales growth to shipment volume growth of approximately $264.2M and favorable pricing of approximately $168.1M, suggesting strength is driven by commercial execution and demand/price rather than measurable liquidity/participant effects typical of strong network platforms.

Circana-reported channel dynamics (tracked retailer channels) show Constellation as a meaningful beer-vendor share gainer: in 2024, it is reported to have gained +1.19 share (and to have 19.58% share of beer category dollars, No. 2 vendor). This implies competitive momentum in a consumer-packaged-goods “share of shelf” sense, not a durable cross-side marketplace network effect.

Constellation states it had multiple “top 15 share gaining brands across the total beer category” in recent filings (e.g., 7 of the top 15 in FY2024; 6 of the top 15 in FY2026), again indicating improving brand share/velocity rather than direct or cross-side network mechanics.
risks: Constellation is not a platform/marketplace business; its core value is driven by brands, distribution, and consumer demand, so any network effects are likely weak, indirect, or not the primary moat driver versus competitors reallocating spend and distribution.

Metrics that would validate strong network effects (e.g., user/participant counts, two-sided liquidity, share-of-wallet with a reinforcing platform loop) are not evident in Constellation’s filings and are not typically reported for CPG brewers, increasing the risk of over- or under-attributing moat to network dynamics.

evidence: Constellation’s enterprise scale is evident in its revenue size of ~$10.0B (FY2024) and ~$10.2B (FY2025), but revenue declined to ~$9.1B (FY2026), limiting the ability of scale to keep compounding cost advantages through volume in the latest year.

Operating leverage from scale shows up directionally: operating margin rose from 30.1% (FY2023) to 33.0% (FY2025) before easing to 31.3% (FY2026), while free cash flow margin remained high at 18.2% (FY2023), 15.2% (FY2024), 19.0% (FY2025), and 19.6% (FY2026).

Beer-sector cost-savings attributable to scale/efficiency initiatives were explicitly quantified: Constellation reported delivering ~$220 million of cost savings through supply chain efficiencies across the Enterprise Beer Business (FY2025).

Cost structure indicates meaningful fixed-cost absorption and some economies of scale, with gross margin (percent of net sales) at 50.4% in FY2024 and rising to 52.1% in FY2025; in FY2024 the company also disclosed that higher cost of product sold was partially offset by favorable fixed cost absorption tied to increased production levels vs. FY2023.

Scale-based market strength reinforces cost leadership potential: Constellation reported holding top share gains and leading imported beer brands in U.S. channels (e.g., Modelo Especial and Corona brands held leading positions by dollar sales/share gains), supported by its large U.S. import/distribution footprint and exclusive/long-lived U.S. rights for key Mexican beer brands.
risks: Scale advantage is not consistently visible through the most recent year: revenue fell from ~$10.2B (FY2025) to ~$9.1B (FY2026) while operating margin eased to 31.3%, suggesting that unit cost advantages can be diluted when volume declines (and/or cost inflation/tariffs rise).

Cost headwinds tied to inputs and policy can overwhelm economies of scale; for example, the company disclosed that FY2024 higher cost of product sold included inflation-impacted materials (malt, aluminum, glass, starch) and global supply chain constraints, and it later cited tariffs on aluminum as a driver of beer cost increases.

bear_case: Constellation Brands’ Beer segment operating income collapsed in FY2026 (operating margin reported at 1.3% vs. 19.5% previously), driven by lower net sales/beer shipment volume and higher cost of product sold rather than purely temporary accounting items.

Constellation Brands reported that FY2026 Beer operating income decline was driven by increased Beer COGS including tariffs on aluminum, indicating input-cost pressure is directly impairing the economics of its branded portfolio rather than being fully offset by pricing.

Beer revenue and operating results show volume sensitivity: FY2026 net sales decreased 10%, and the 10-K attributes the Beer net sales decline primarily to shipment volume decline (partially offset by pricing), which is inconsistent with consistently strong pricing power stabilizing demand.

Constellation’s medium-term capacity parity still depends on long-cycle brewery build progress (Veracruz initial production expected around mid-FY2027), meaning execution risk could delay recovery if demand trends or competitive supply terms worsen before new capacity comes online.

stocks.investment_implication: PPG’s narrow, stable moat, rated 5.9, rests on pricing power and barriers created by manufacturing investment and customer qualification. Its 12.5% return on invested capital and positive operating margins and free cash flow in each year provide adequate support, though they do not prove excess returns. The moat looks durable but limited, given fluctuating margins and modest revenue growth.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: PPG’s operating margin rose from 10.7% in 2022 to 13.7% in 2025, consistent with some pricing and portfolio discipline.
stocks.key_risk: Pricing pressure, including lower index-based prices in some customer contracts, could erode PPG’s margins and weaken its moat.

evidence: PPG’s operating margin increased from 10.7% (FY2022) to 13.7% (FY2023), then 14.4% (FY2024), before easing to 13.7% (FY2025), indicating mid-cycle resilience consistent with some pricing/portfolio discipline rather than pure volume growth.
PPG’s net margin rose from 6.6% (FY2022) to 7.8% (FY2023) and 7.0% (FY2024), then jumped to 9.9% (FY2025), suggesting better cost capture / pricing realization in the most recent year of the series.

Across FY2022–FY2025, PPG’s reported FCF margin was volatile but improved from 3.1% (FY2022) to 11.7% (FY2023), fell to 4.4% (FY2024), and recovered to 7.3% (FY2025), consistent with pricing partly offsetting cost/working-capital swings rather than sustained erosion.

PPG demonstrates active selling-price management: in 2024 annual reporting, PPG disclosed cost-of-sales as a % of net sales improved to 58.4% in FY2024 from 59.6% in FY2023, attributing changes to moderating raw material costs and lower sales volume (i.e., margin not solely driven by input costs).

Brand strength indicators exist at the category level: PPG is ranked #2 in the chemical industry on Fortune’s “World’s Most Admired Companies” list (PPG press release), supporting that the company’s brand has strong reputation, though this is not a direct churn/retention metric.
risks: PPG’s margins are not consistently expanding over the full 3–5 year window (operating margin and FCF margin both decline in FY2024 vs FY2023), which weakens evidence for durable, high pricing power.

There is no company-specific public evidence in the searched sources of measurable customer loyalty metrics (e.g., NPS, stated repeat-purchase rates, churn/retention) or quantified premium pricing vs specific competitors; without this, the “brand loyalty” portion of pricing power is under-supported.

PPG operates in specialty chemicals/coatings with contract- and index-linked elements; in its 2025 annual reporting, it noted industrial coatings organic sales decreased due to lower selling prices, including impacts from lower index-based prices under certain customer contracts—an explicit channel for pricing pressure.

evidence: PPG’s capital intensity remains high for specialty coatings: capital expenditures were $486M (2022), $516M (2023), and $721M (2024), implying a material ongoing fixed-asset spending requirement for capacity and environmental control upgrades.

PPG planned further large-scale spending, stating that during 2025 capital expenditures were expected to be approximately $725M to $775M—supporting the view that sustained investment is needed to compete at scale in its operating footprint.

PPG is still allocating substantial investment to new manufacturing: it announced a $380M investment to build a new U.S. aerospace coatings and sealants manufacturing facility (Shelby, North Carolina), illustrating that scaling into specialized coatings can require hundreds of millions in upfront CAPEX.

Regulatory/compliance-related qualification and quality-system requirements can slow competitive entry in downstream coatings: for example, PPG’s supplier quality documentation indicates ISO 9001:2015 certification and supplier QMS expectations/validation as requirements tied to business opportunities (noting the company’s supplier qualification and audit approach).

PPG’s overall economics do not appear to be driven by single-expiry patent exclusivity: the available evidence found here is more consistent with durable barriers from manufacturing scale, ongoing CAPEX, and customer qualification cycles rather than clearly documented near-term patent cliffs (no reliable patent count/expiry timeline data was captured in the sources retrieved).
risks: The barrier score may be understated or overstated because the evidence gathered here did not include reliable, company-specific patent portfolio counts and a dated patent expiry/coverage timeline; without that, the IP-driven component of barriers cannot be measured directly.

Regulatory/qualification claims may not constitute true “entry barriers” against new manufacturers at the firm level; they may instead affect the speed of customer-by-customer qualification rather than blocking entry entirely.

PPG’s documented CAPEX levels reflect industry capital needs, but high incumbent spending does not automatically prevent a well-funded entrant from catching up within a few years if it can secure feedstocks, customers, and qualification approvals.

evidence: PPG participates in workflow/operational lock-in in automotive refinish via the PPG MOONWALK® automated paint mixing system and related digital tools (e.g., PPG LINQ™), with MOONWALK requiring installations and training for shop adoption (PPG has expanded installations, including a claim of reaching a 3,000th installation at a customer location).

PPG uses certified technician/distributor programs that create switching friction: PPG automotive refinish technicians must recertify every two years via a 1-day recertification course, and PPG distributor technical representatives have a certification program that includes two courses and a two-day hands-on performance evaluation (with DTRC status tied to PPG certification programs and eligibility).

In its automotive refinish distributor ecosystem, PPG creates economic/commitment friction through contractual distributor milestones: a PPG Platinum Distributor agreement requires, among other items, yearly distributor purchases of $250,000, plus specific program milestones including purchasing inventory and having a shop conversion element (e.g., a signed contract for a PPG MOONWALK™ system at a customer/distributor location).

PPG’s technical service model is structured to embed into customer operations, including personalized technical support and a focus on improving customer coating operations (PPG describes providing technical support and assessing a customer’s entire coating operation to increase efficiency and reduce waste).

On the contract-structure dimension, PPG operates within the coatings industry with multi-year supply arrangements: an older ICI/Glidden/PPG SEC filing states that PPG “enter[s] into multi-year supply agreements with many of our largest customers,” indicating that multi-year contracting is an available mechanism for switching friction (though this source is not PPG-specific to today’s contract terms).
risks: No publicly verifiable, PPG-specific customer churn/retention metrics are cited in the sources found; without churn/retention, the real magnitude of switching costs (how often customers attempt switching and how costly it is in practice) cannot be quantified.

Switching friction is likely heterogeneous across PPG segments (automotive refinish vs. industrial coatings vs. aerospace/protective & marine); the evidence found is strongest in the refinish/distributor ecosystem and weaker on proprietary formats/data portability and measurable migration costs for end customers.
The multi-year supply-agreement evidence located is from an older SEC filing (not confirmed to reflect current PPG contract lengths, termination fees, or minimum-commitment structures).

evidence: PPG’s refinish coatings “digital ecosystem” (PPG LINQ™) and related hardware have measurable scale: PPG reported its PPG MOONWALK® automated paint mixing system reached the 3,000th global installation milestone in August 2025, and that MoonWalk is used by collision centers in more than 60 countries.

PPG indicated growing penetration of its installed base prior to that: in 2024 PPG reported MOONWALK systems installed in more than 2,300 body shops worldwide and that it had customers in all 50 U.S. states.

In Q3 2025 earnings call commentary, PPG stated it grew the number of refinish LINQ subscriptions and increased Moonwalk hardware installations to “more than 3,000,” linking the installed base/subscriptions to customer productivity and “related share gains.”

PPG’s core financial outcomes over 2022–2025 show only modest top-line growth (revenue CAGR ~0.6%) while profitability fluctuated (operating margin 10.7% in 2022 rising to 14.4% in 2024, then 13.7% in 2025), suggesting any network-effect reinforcement is not yet visible as a consistently accelerating margin profile in the overall company.
risks: PPG is primarily a coatings and specialty chemicals supplier (not a pure software marketplace), so cross-side/marketplace liquidity network effects are not clearly evidenced at the company-wide level versus customer productivity benefits from connected refinish tooling (direct effects are more plausible than two-sided liquidity effects).

Competitors in coatings/finishes (e.g., other major global coatings companies) can replicate digital workflow and technical services; the durability of LINQ/MOONWALK network effects depends on sustained installed-base growth and switching costs rather than being inherent to chemistry supply alone.

Reported company-wide revenue growth has been low (CAGR ~0.6% from 2022–2025), which reduces the evidence that network effects are driving accelerating demand across the full portfolio rather than only in the automotive refinish niche.

evidence: PPG is large enough to run at scale (net sales of $15.6B in 2022, $16.2B in 2023, $15.8B in 2024, and $15.9B in 2025), but revenue is essentially flat across 2022–2025 (≈0.6% CAGR), which limits strong evidence of steadily widening cost gaps via volume expansion.

Operating leverage is mixed: operating margin was 10.7% (2022) → 13.7% (2023) → 14.4% (2024) → 13.7% (2025), consistent with some ability to convert sales into profit, but not a consistent multi-year widening trend that would strongly evidence scale-driven unit-cost advantage.

Cost structure shows some manufacturing productivity/cost control translating into unit economics, but still with a cost base that moves with inflation: for 2025 vs. 2024, PPG reported cost of sales (exclusive of depreciation and amortization) of $9,316M vs. $9,252M (+0.7%) while cost of sales as a % of net sales rose slightly to 58.7% (from 58.4%). PPG attributes cost changes partly to increased manufacturing productivity and divestitures, but the margin math does not show a clear, structural step-down in unit costs.

PPG has active cost programs that can be consistent with scale benefits (e.g., a comprehensive cost reduction program approved in October 2024 with anticipated annualized pre-tax savings of ~$175M once fully implemented), yet this is a restructuring/cost actions story rather than direct proof that competitors are structurally unable to match PPG’s unit economics.

PPG’s spending profile suggests it is not a lowest-cost producer through 'thin' operating overhead: selling, general and administrative expenses were 21.4% of net sales in 2023 and 21.7% in 2025 (with 2024 shown at 21.4% in the filing excerpt), while R&D is ~2.8% of net sales in 2024 (2.7% in 2023, 2.9% in 2022), implying meaningful scale but not an overhead-minimization strategy that would typically accompany extreme unit-cost leadership.
risks: PPG’s margins and cost-of-sales ratios fluctuate with macro and restructuring/divestiture effects (flat revenue CAGR and cost-of-sales % changing only slightly), which makes it hard to attribute unit-cost leadership specifically to scale rather than cycle-specific pricing, mix, or one-time actions.

Specialty chemicals/coatings often involve localized production, logistics, and customer-qualification constraints; even large incumbents may not fully suppress unit costs versus other large players (e.g., other global coating producers), limiting the durability of scale advantages over a 10-year horizon.

bear_case: PPG’s total revenue was essentially flat to slightly down across FY2022–FY2025 (USD 15.6B → 16.2B → 15.8B → 15.9B), providing no evidence of compounding moat-driven demand growth.

PPG’s operating margin fell from 14.4% in FY2024 to 13.7% in FY2025, and its free-cash-flow margin collapsed from 11.7% in FY2023 to 4.4% in FY2024 before partially recovering to 7.3% in FY2025—this volatility is consistent with competitive pricing/mix pressure rather than steadily strengthening moat economics.

PPG disclosed that its Industrial Coatings segment organic sales declined in 2024 due to lower selling prices, including the impact of lower index-based prices under certain customer contracts—i.e., contract-indexing mechanisms that can mechanically transmit pricing pressure to the business.

PPG’s reported cash-generation effectiveness improved in FY2025 (FCF margin 7.3%) but was not sustained across the full FY2022–FY2025 period (3.1% in FY2022, 11.7% in FY2023, 4.4% in FY2024), weakening the case that pricing power and cost advantages are structurally persistent through cycles.

stocks.investment_implication: CRH’s narrow, eroding moat rests on pricing power and economies of scale in its building-materials operations. Its 10.6% return on invested capital and operating margin increase from 11.5% in 2022 to 14.2% in 2025 provide adequate financial support, but competitive pressure and cyclical pricing make the advantage vulnerable over time.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: CRH’s continued pricing momentum helped lift its operating margin to 14.2% in 2025.
stocks.key_risk: Competition and cyclical demand could weaken CRH’s pricing power and compress its margins.

evidence: CRH’s operating margin expanded from 11.5% (FY2022) to 14.2% (FY2025), a +2.7 percentage-point improvement over 4 years, consistent with sustained pricing/portfolio advantage rather than pure cost normalization.
CRH’s net margin moved from 9.0% (FY2023) to 10.0% (FY2025) after a 2023 trough, indicating profitability resilience while it still grew revenue from $34.9bn (FY2023) to $37.4bn (FY2025).

CRH reported an explicit improvement in gross profit margin: 34.2% in FY2024 (up from 33.1% in FY2023), attributing the increase to revenue growth exceeding increases in total cost of revenues (i.e., mix/price outpacing cost pressure).
CRH’s FY2025 results commentary cited “continued pricing momentum” as a driver of higher profitability (Adjusted EBITDA increased to $7.7bn in FY2025, and margin improved vs FY2024).

CRH’s sustainability reporting states it completed customer surveys with “above average levels of satisfaction” at 86% (FY2022), 89% (FY2023), and 89% (FY2024), supporting customer stickiness/brand preference signals in its customer-connected solutions approach.
risks: CRH itself discloses that if it fails to maintain pricing in an inflationary environment or differentiate from competitors, financial performance could be adversely impacted—highlighting the risk that pricing power is not guaranteed.

The building materials market (aggregates, cementitious materials, readymixed concrete, asphalt) is structurally cyclical and can price competitively in downturns; margins can compress even if customer satisfaction remains high.

CRH’s customer-satisfaction data reflects “above average satisfaction” but does not provide direct, company-specific churn/repeat-purchase rates; brand-loyalty moat strength may be harder to quantify than margin outcomes.

evidence: CRH’s capital intensity for maintaining/expanding core production assets is substantial: 2024 capital expenditure was $2.6 billion and 2025 capital expenditure was $2.7 billion (i.e., a multi‑billion annual spending requirement to sustain supply and footprint).

CRH is highly asset-backed and vertically integrated through ownership/control of scarce raw-material sources: CRH describes its businesses as resource-backed via an extensive network of quarry locations that supply aggregates for downstream concrete/asphalt operations (ownership/control of mineral deposits materially raises the effective entry barrier versus pure distributors).

Regulatory and permitting requirements meaningfully constrain incremental supply additions for quarries/mines and related production: CRH states that it is required to obtain operating permits and resource rights (e.g., water rights) to conduct operations such as quarries, mines, and production/distribution facilities.

CRH evidences scale acquisition as its primary growth path rather than greenfield replication: in 2024 it completed 40 acquisitions with total cash consideration of $5.0 billion (including a $2.1 billion cement/readymixed concrete portfolio in Texas and $787 million acquisition of a majority stake in Adbri), indicating that credible market expansion typically requires large up-front balance-sheet capacity and site-specific assets rather than rapid organic entry.
risks: Patent/IP barriers are not evidenced with hard metrics here (e.g., patent counts, specific families, and expiry schedule were not located in the available sources), so if CRH’s defensibility relies less on IP and more on assets/regulation, the true entry barrier may be lower than a strong IP-driven score.

Building materials (aggregates/cement/concrete/asphalt) remain fundamentally supply-and-cost driven; competitors can enter by acquiring existing plants/leases or reconfiguring capacity (as suggested by CRH’s own frequent acquisition activity in the sector), which can cap how high barriers can realistically be.

evidence: CRH reports that it serves projects via construction contracts that are often multi-year, but the company’s disclosures show typical construction working-capital lock-in via retentions and unbilled amounts (e.g., contract assets from unbilled revenue and customer retentions were $299 million as of Dec. 31, 2025 and $226 million as of Dec. 31, 2024; and $3,114 million of remaining transaction price was expected to close within ~12 months).

CRH’s value proposition is largely operational scale and “connected portfolio” supply-chain coverage (e.g., vertically integrated quarries and production of aggregates/cement/asphalt/readymixed concrete/concrete products), which supports repeat business but is not the same as proprietary ecosystem/data integration that would make switching technically hard.

CRH explicitly discloses that it operates in highly competitive, fragmented markets where products/services face strong competition and that profits are sensitive to volumes/prices impacted by competitive conditions—conditions that imply customers can substitute suppliers rather than being locked in by switching-friction barriers.

CRH’s most direct “exit friction” evidence in filings appears to be financial exposure on project timelines (contract assets/contract liabilities, retentions withheld until acceptance, and timing of billings/advance payments), rather than contractual termination penalties or long-term take-or-pay arrangements that would persistently raise migration cost for customers.
risks: The filings reviewed do not provide customer-level churn/retention rates or explicit contract termination/indemnity penalties (or minimum commitments), so the switching-cost score may understate any hidden contract-structure friction (e.g., local pricing agreements, sole-source arrangements, or multi-year supply commitments).

CRH’s “customer-connected solutions” positioning could involve deeper integration on certain project types (e.g., bespoke mixes, technical specifications, or project management workflows), but the evidence retrieved here did not quantify the migration cost/time or interoperability/data portability barriers needed to validate high switching costs.

evidence: CRH’s operating footprint is large but geographically distributed rather than a consumer/social platform: as of December 31, 2024 it reported 3,816 operating locations.

CRH does not show measurable direct or cross-side marketplace network effects (e.g., buyers/sellers on a platform); instead its integration is physical/supply-chain oriented (“integrating materials, products and services… drive repeat business”), which is not the same as user-count driven network value.

Over the last 3–5 years, user/participant counts relevant to network effects are not presented as a scaling driver; CRH’s workforce is large and broadly steady (e.g., average employees at each location: 24 in 2022 vs 21 in 2024, indicating no clear “more participants make product better” dynamic).

CRH’s segment scale is reinforced by assets and capacity (e.g., 1,296 mining properties and 246,058 acres owned plus 129,818 acres leased as of Dec 31, 2024), which supports local supply reliability but is not a classic network effect (value increasing with additional users on the same platform).
risks: CRH’s 'repeat business' could partially reflect switching costs and relationships with contractors that increase with scale, but the company does not quantify this as network effects tied to customer count growth.

Network-like reinforcement could exist in customer contracting ecosystems (e.g., preferred supplier arrangements), but there is no publicly cited metric (liquidity, platform participation, share-of-wallet, or accelerating participant growth) in the sourced materials to demonstrate network effects rather than operational scale.

evidence: Scale is reflected in CRH’s very large revenue base (US$32.7bn in 2022, US$34.9bn in 2023, US$35.6bn in 2024, US$37.4bn in 2025) and consistently strong operating profitability (operating margin 11.5% in 2022, 12.8% in 2023, 13.8% in 2024, 14.2% in 2025).

Operating leverage consistent with scale/utilization: gross profit grew from US$10.815bn (2022) to US$11.963bn (2023) to US$12.701bn (2024) while total cost of revenues was roughly flat-to-down (total cost of revenues US$21.908bn in 2022, US$22.986bn in 2023, US$22.871bn in 2024), and the gross margin rose to 35.7% in 2024 from 34.2% in 2023 (up 150 bps) with management citing cost control and operational efficiencies.

SG&A intensity supports that fixed/scale costs are being absorbed effectively: SG&A was US$7.056bn in 2022, US$7.486bn in 2023, and US$7.852bn in 2024, while total revenues rose to US$35.572bn in 2024; management characterizes SG&A as largely haulage and labor-driven, implying that the company’s scale and operating density help manage these costs versus throughput.

Market leadership positions are explicitly linked by management to “scale” and show concentration in the very core of building materials: CRH reports #1 positions in key North American aggregates and critical infrastructure categories and #1 Concrete Products and #1 Asphalt in its presentation, and #3 Cement in North America & Europe (market leadership positions based on annualized sales volumes).

Economies of supply-chain/logistics from a dense footprint: CRH states it operates at 2,127 locations across 48 U.S. states and seven Canadian provinces (Americas) and 1,834 locations across 27 countries (International) and reports very large internal and external volumes (e.g., annualized aggregates sales 380.7 million tons in 2025), which supports that the company can spread fixed costs (quarry/plant logistics, procurement, distribution) over higher tonnage—key to unit cost advantage in aggregates/cement.
risks: Commodity/materials pricing and energy inputs remain major drivers of unit costs; CRH’s own reporting attributes part of cost changes to energy price declines (e.g., 2024 total cost of revenues decreased primarily with an 18% decrease in energy costs), which means scale benefits may be partly cyclical rather than purely structural.

Competitive cost gaps may not be structural if regional peers (e.g., large aggregates/cement operators) have similar asset density in specific corridors; absent detailed unit-cost disclosures versus top rivals, the magnitude of CRH’s true cost-per-ton advantage cannot be precisely quantified from public filings.

bear_case: CRH is facing a current, government-led antitrust civil merger case in the U.S. involving CRH plc and named operating subsidiaries, indicating regulators view parts of its building-materials footprint as capable of raising competition concerns.

CRH’s own reported profitability does not show sustained moat durability across the cycle: operating margin increased from 11.5% (FY2022) to 14.2% (FY2025), but net margin dipped materially to 9.0% in FY2023 before only partially recovering to 10.0% by FY2025, consistent with episodic margin erosion typical of contested, price-sensitive building-materials markets.

CRH repeatedly emphasizes pricing and competitive conditions as key drivers and admits that competitors can expand positions and that CRH can face competition for acquisitions—undercutting the claim of entrenched, hard-to-attack structural advantage.

CRH’s growth strategy relies heavily on acquisition scale (e.g., $5.0B acquisition consideration in 2024) rather than demonstrating defensible, internally generated “moat” economics that would persist without balance-sheet-enabled buying, implying barrier strength is partly acquisition-driven and therefore contestable.
