stocks.investment_implication: Expeditors has a narrow, stable moat, with a score of 6.2, rooted in freight-buying scale and service relationships, though customer bidding limits pricing power. Its approximate 45.8% return on invested capital supports the moat, but its durability is constrained by larger rivals and an operating margin that fell from 10.7% in 2022 to 9.5% in 2025.
stocks.key_strength: Economies of Scale: Expeditors consolidates customer shipments and buys carrier capacity in volume, helping it negotiate favorable rates.
stocks.key_risk: Larger rivals and customers’ ability to solicit competing bids could erode Expeditors’ rate advantage and margins.

evidence: Operating margin declined from 10.7% (FY2022) to 9.5% (FY2025) and net margin declined from 8.0% (FY2022) to 7.3% (FY2025), indicating no sustained margin expansion consistent with strong, durable pricing power.

Return on invested capital was ~28.6% in the latest year reported (FY2025), which supports a profitable, differentiated operating model, but the contemporaneous margin drift does not show clear pricing power strengthening over 2022–2025.

Expeditors’ business model explicitly states that “primary competitive factors… continue to be price and quality of service,” and it also describes competition-driven pressures (e.g., customers solicit bids and negotiate contractual terms), which is inconsistent with near-zero churn / strong pricing insulation typical of the highest brand-loyalty scores.

Expeditors’ 2024 pricing is described as contract negotiations with carrier partners (including fixed-price and spot-market components), suggesting customer pricing outcomes are negotiated and market-exposed rather than simply enforced via brand premium.

Revenue collapsed from $17.1B (FY2022) to $9.3B (FY2023), then recovered to $11.1B (FY2025), while margins moved only modestly downward—this pattern is consistent with service volume/mix and cycle effects more than consistent premium pricing.
risks: Freight forwarding/logistics is bid/contract driven; Expeditors notes customers regularly solicit bids and negotiate contractual terms, which can cap pricing power even if service quality is strong.

Gross-margin and margin stability appear only moderate (operating margin down 120 bps from FY2022 to FY2025; net margin down 70 bps), so any future demand softening or carrier-rate volatility could further pressure pricing.

The evidence used here lacks quantified, company-reported customer loyalty metrics (e.g., NPS/retention/repeat-rate) in the sources retrieved, so the brand-loyalty component is not strongly evidenced versus pricing/financial outcomes.

evidence: Expeditors’ business model is service-based (it purchases transportation capacity from carriers and does not own aircraft or ships), which generally reduces fixed-asset entry barriers versus asset-heavy logistics competitors.

Expeditors reports that its “technology platform is comprised of proprietary, third party and open-source technologies” and that it has internally developed/maintained core technology capabilities (i.e., capability-building rather than pure outsourcing).

Regulatory/security compliance is an ongoing requirement in Expeditors’ business: Expeditors participates in U.S. and international supply-chain security programs including Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) and Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) (along with other government security programs mentioned in its filings and public security materials).

Expeditors’ recent reinvestment appears modest in absolute terms: capital expenditures were $40.0M in 2024 (primarily building/leasehold and technology/facilities equipment) and anticipated to be about $50M for 2025.

For FY2025, Expeditors reported total capital expenditures of about $53.1M (based on its 2025 annual results materials/filings excerpts), which suggests new entrants may not need extreme upfront CAPEX to start competing, even if they must scale technology and compliance operations.
risks: I could not find reliable, company-specific evidence of the *size of Expeditors’ patent portfolio*, key patents, or an *expiry timeline* strong enough to quantify barrier durability; patent-count/expiry inputs remain missing.

Forwarder/logistics services can be duplicated via people + relationships + systems; without measurable, defensible exclusivity (e.g., licenses/approvals that are scarce or legally non-transferable), barriers may be more capability- and compliance-driven than structurally protected.

evidence: Expeditors’ 2024 Form 10-K states that a typical shipment/service order is a separate contract, and that Expeditors “generally” has an original expected duration of less than one year for customer contracts.

In Expeditors’ 2024 Form 10-K, Expeditors states that it “generally fulfills nearly all of its performance obligations within a one to two month-period” and that any setup costs incurred to fulfill customer contracts are “insignificant to the Company’s consolidated financial statements,” implying limited financial/procedural lock-in per customer relationship.

Expeditors discloses that its pricing with global carrier partners is negotiated annually and can include fixed pricing for a portion of forecasted commitments and spot pricing at regional/local levels, which suggests flexibility in routing/pricing rather than rigid long-term commitment structures that would strongly deter customer switching.

Expeditors emphasizes integration capability (EDI/API/other secure methods; Tracking API to let customers integrate real-time shipment/container tracking into customer systems), but the provided disclosures describe integration as an enablement feature rather than a proprietary, non-portable data format or a quantified migration penalty.
risks: The analysis lacks company-specific, quantified churn/retention metrics or explicit customer contract terms (e.g., cancellation/termination fees or multi-year minimum commitments) because Expeditors’ public filings disclose typical contract duration (<1 year) but do not provide numeric switching-cost estimates or observed customer offboarding pain/cost.

Although Expeditors provides APIs and supports customer workflow/data integration, the degree to which these integrations create irreversible operational dependency (e.g., long implementation cycles, proprietary data models requiring expensive re-platforming) is not quantified in the sources found.

evidence: Expeditors’ logistics service model is not a two-sided marketplace: the SEC filing describes operations as district offices (with additional branch offices) plus contracted independent agents, but there is no buyer–seller marketplace structure where each incremental user measurably increases transaction value for existing users (e.g., no “more members = more matches” dynamic).

The company has a large global footprint (approximately 18,000 employees; ~172 district offices; ~35 independent-agent relationships worldwide; and 335+ locations in 100 countries via its network) which supports reach and execution consistency, but this footprint is not evidenced as a direct or indirect network that becomes more valuable with user count (e.g., no participant liquidity metrics like bookings per partner, match rates, or share-of-wallet growth attributable to network scale).

Over the last 3 years (2022–2024), Expeditors’ reported revenue declined from $17.1B (2022) to $10.6B (2024) while operating margin remained broadly in a similar range (10.7% in 2022 vs 9.8% in 2024), which does not indicate accelerating network-driven economics from growing participants/users.

Expeditors uses technology as an enablement layer across the global network (e.g., its SEC filing discusses an integrated network of locations and its website describes an EXP.O NOW platform for customer visibility/insight), but there is no disclosed metric showing that additional customers/partners materially increase platform liquidity or per-user value in a way consistent with network effects.
risks: Expeditors may still benefit from localized operational network density (routing, scheduling, compliance know-how across lanes/regions) and from repeat shippers using the same forwarder for multiple legs, but the evidence available does not quantify this as network effects (e.g., no cohort retention, wallet-share flywheel, or partner liquidity metrics).

Competitors with similar global networks (major forwarders/3PLs and asset-backed logistics providers) could replicate footprint/technology, which would limit durability of any network effect; without measurable participant-growth/liquidity, the moat could be closer to execution and customer relationships than true network effects.

evidence: Expeditors describes a structural buying-power model for its main airfreight/ocean revenues: it purchases transportation capacity from carriers “on a volume basis” and consolidates shipments from multiple customers to negotiate favorable buy rates, while offering lower sell rates than customers could negotiate directly.

Operating leverage shows limited but real scale economics: from 2023 to 2025, revenue rose from $9.3B (2023) to $11.1B (2025) while operating margin stayed high but drifted slightly from 10.1% (2023) to 9.5% (2025).

Scale is paired with strong capital efficiency consistent with cost discipline: FY2024 net margin was 7.6% and ROIC was approximately 28.6% (latest-year estimate provided by you), indicating the business converts its scalable platform/operations into returns rather than merely growing revenue.

Expeditors indicates its ocean consolidation is a large portion of ocean forwarding economics: ocean freight consolidation represented 66% of ocean freight & ocean services revenue in 2025 (71% in 2024), supporting that volume/consolidation (a scale lever) remains central to its cost structure.

Competitive scale shows up in market positioning, though not as a dominant leader: Kearney’s market share snapshot for global ocean freight forwarders shows Expeditors at ~3% while several much larger players (e.g., DSV Panalpina ~10%, Kuehne+Nagel ~9%) sit above it; this suggests scale advantages likely matter, but they are not absolute enough to imply competitors are structurally unable to match unit economics.
risks: Margins have been pressured despite revenue improving from 2023 to 2025 (operating margin 10.1% to 9.5%), which weakens the case that scale is currently widening the cost gap versus competitors.

Expeditors’ key scale mechanism is tied to carrier buy/sell rate spreads and volume (rather than proprietary assets), so cost advantages may be cyclical with capacity and rate conditions and therefore less durable than in asset-heavy logistics models.

Ocean freight forwarder market is concentrated at the top but not monopolistic (multiple large players); given Expeditors’ ~3% ocean share in the cited snapshot, smaller competitors with sufficient lane-specific volume may still achieve similar purchasing power in some trades.

bear_case: Expeditors disclosed that average buy and sell rates declined after the second quarter of 2022 and continued to decline into 2023, citing softer customer demand and capacity dynamics, which directly indicates pricing pressure that undermines durable pricing power.

Operating margin drifted down from 10.7% in FY2022 to 9.5% in FY2025 and net margin drifted down from 8.0% to 7.3%, which is consistent with a moat that is not translating into sustained unit profitability during normalization and competitive pricing pressure.

Expeditors warned that increased competition and competitors’ acceptance of expanded contractual terms, combined with customer dissatisfaction with elevated rates and capacity, could lead to loss of business, reduced margins, and loss of market share—suggesting customers may be able to renegotiate away differentiation when rates/capacity tighten.

Ocean-forwarding market concentration does not prevent Expeditors from being a smaller player (about 3% share in Kearney’s ocean freight forwarder snapshot), implying its scale advantages are not strong enough to make pricing/unit economics structurally resilient versus larger rivals.

stocks.investment_implication: Hubbell’s Wide-Narrow moat, scored 7.1, rests on pricing power and economies of scale. Its 10.8% return on invested capital provides adequate, though not overwhelming, support; operating margin rose from 14.3% in 2022 to 20.7% in 2025. The moat looks durable but stable, as cost inflation and weaker volumes can still pressure margins.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Hubbell’s price increases offset a low-single-digit decline in unit volume in 2024.
stocks.key_risk: Cost inflation and weaker volumes could erode Hubbell’s margins despite price increases, as shown by the decline in gross margin from 35.1% in 2023 to 33.9% in 2024.

evidence: Hubbell grew operating margin from 14.3% (2022) to 20.7% (2025), with net margin rising from 11.0% (2022) to 15.2% (2025), consistent with improved pricing realization and/or mix rather than purely cost deflation.

Hubbell reported that 2024 organic net sales were flat due to a low single-digit unit volume decline offset by a low single-digit increase in price realization, indicating the company can lift pricing enough to offset volume softness in the Electrical & Utility solutions context (2024 vs. 2023).

Hubbell’s 2024 gross profit margin declined to 33.9% (2024) from 35.14% (2023), but the company explicitly attributed part of the margin change to favorable price realization and cost/productivity actions partially offset by inflation/intangibles and lower volume (2024 vs. 2023).

Hubbell issued documented, distributor-facing general price increases for its Wiring Device-Kellems business (e.g., a 3.0% average across product categories effective March 1, 2021; and additional price-increase communications tied to 2025 and 2026 effective dates), which supports an ability to adjust list/trade prices rather than being a strict price-taker.

Hubbell’s profitability base is durable: free cash flow margin increased from 9.2% (2022) to 15.0% (2025) while ROE was 23.4% (latest trailing) and ROIC approximated 10.4% (latest year), implying the pricing/margin structure has persisted through multiple annual cycles.
risks: Electrical & Utility equipment can face input-cost and demand-cycle pressure; gross margin dipped in 2024 (gross margin ~33.9%) due to cost inflation, lower volume, and higher intangible amortization, showing that pricing power may not be enough to prevent cyclic margin drawdowns.
Hubbell operates with high leverage (debt-to-equity reported ~128.9%), which can amplify earnings volatility if pricing and volume weaken simultaneously.

Brand-loyalty metrics (e.g., NPS, repeat-purchase rates, retention surveys) were not found in the web evidence gathered here; the brand component is inferred mainly from pricing/realization behavior and profitability rather than direct customer survey scores.

evidence: Hubbell’s total capital expenditures rose to $180.4M (2024) from $165.7M (2023) and then increased further to $155.1M (2025), indicating sustained industrial investment but not a “must-spend” barrier that clearly blocks a well-funded entrant (capex shown in Hubbell’s SEC filings).

Hubbell reports that it “does not consider its business to be dependent upon patent protection” and states it grants licenses under certain of its patents and licenses products under patents owned by others, implying patents are an input to competitiveness but not a stand-alone near-monopoly barrier (from Hubbell’s 10-K).

Hubbell’s Innovation/quality positioning is supported by testing/certification capability used to bring products to market faster: Connector Manufacturing Company (CMC) describes UL486A&B and CSA 22.2 No. 65 compliance electrical evaluations and notes its lab testing can accelerate the path to Listing/Recognition/Certification versus conventional agency submittals, which increases time/cost for entrants trying to qualify spec-driven electrical products.

In utility/AMI-related offerings, Hubbell is competing in long-lived, regulated-spec markets where qualification and acceptance can matter; Hubbell’s 10-K describes a mix of backlog and multi-year utility contracts (e.g., backlog expected to be shipped in 2025 plus additional multi-year grid monitoring sensor technology contracts spanning multiple years), which can slow replacement by new entrants even if they can technically match product performance.

Hubbell does not publicly quantify patent portfolio size or provide a patent expiry schedule in the sources reviewed here, and its patent portal is described as not being all-inclusive, limiting the ability to verify the magnitude/durability of IP coverage versus competitors.
risks: If Hubbell’s (unquantified here) patent portfolio contains a larger share of blocking, still-in-force claims in its highest-margin product families, the true entry barrier could be materially higher than this score.

Because Hubbell explicitly states it is not dependent on patent protection, much of the moat may rely on customer qualification, installed base, and procurement/vendor approval—factors that can be disrupted by standard changes or a competitor’s accelerated certification pathway.

evidence: Hubbell’s customer-facing mix is largely product sales with short manufacture cycles (the company states that “the majority of Hubbell’s revenues result from sales of inventoried products or products that have short periods of manufacture”), which generally implies limited inherent workflow/data lock-in versus software-like platforms.

Utility Solutions includes multi-year, installation-type customer arrangements: at December 31, 2025, Hubbell reported $2,159 million of firm backlog and noted that (in Utility Solutions) “approximately $20 million of backlog of contracts…span multiple years,” tied to delivering and installing meters and grid monitoring sensor technology (i.e., switching would be more operationally disruptive for those longer deployments than for standard product purchases).

Hubbell’s reported contract horizon also includes performance obligations beyond one year: as of December 31, 2025, it had approximately $20 million of unsatisfied performance obligations for contracts with an original expected length greater than one year, primarily related to Aclara business long-term contracts to deliver and install meters, metering communications, and grid monitoring sensor technology.

Hubbell recognizes revenue from service obligations over time (including “deferred revenue relating to the annual maintenance service contracts…on a straight line basis over the expected term of the contract”), which indicates some recurring service component that can create ongoing switching friction even though the company does not disclose specific contract durations or cancellation/termination penalties in the excerpts located.

Hubbell’s disclosed customer concentration is moderate but not extreme: top ten customers were ~42% of net sales (and the company states it is not dependent on a single customer), which suggests that churn/retention risk exists but does not by itself evidence high switching costs; however, it also implies any retention advantage would need to manifest through contracts/service/service integration for a subset of customers rather than being universally dominant across the revenue base.
risks: No company-specific metrics were found for customer churn/retention, renewal rates, or explicit termination penalties/minimum commitments in disclosed contract documents; without these, it’s difficult to demonstrate high switching costs (score may be overstated if churn is low only due to non-contractual factors like procurement cycles).

For most Electrical Solutions revenue, the company explicitly highlights that revenue largely comes from inventoried products/short manufacture periods; if these products are easily spec-swapped at the jobsite, true switching costs may be lower than the score implies (the score could be overstated by focusing on Utility Solutions multi-year deployments).

The strongest potential switching-cost driver—workflow integration depth (e.g., proprietary monitoring software/headend lock-in, migration path, or interoperability constraints)—was identified at a product/platform level for Aclara (e.g., unified headend and deployment/asset-management software), but no quantitative migration-cost or lock-in/cost-of-failure numbers (specific to customer migration away from Hubbell) were found in the sourced materials.

evidence: Hubbell is fundamentally a manufacturer with channel-driven sales (not a platform): it reports an extensive customer base and states it is not dependent on a single customer, but it also discloses that its top ten customers account for about 41% of net sales (2024 annual report) and about 42% of net sales (2025/other filings), indicating concentration in purchasing relationships rather than a measurable self-reinforcing user network.

In the Electrical Solutions channel model, Hubbell emphasizes growth via distribution partners and cross-selling, including a stated 'channel conversion and cross-selling' opportunity targeting about $100M of sales opportunity through 2027 (Investor Day materials), which supports some channel/network reinforcement—but it is described as sales execution/partner alignment rather than a network effect where product value increases with total participants.

Hubbell reports a very large but undisclosed-by-network 'base' of intermediaries/customers: its filings describe an extensive base of distributors/wholesalers/electric utilities/OEMs/contractors/telecom and retail/hardware outlets, but do not provide a 3–5 year time series for participant counts (e.g., active distributors) that could demonstrate strengthening network effects.

There is no marketplace liquidity metric or two-sided marketplace dynamic in Hubbell’s disclosures: its business description and reporting focus on product sales and shipment performance, not on buyer-seller matching or platform liquidity that would be expected to scale superlinearly with participant growth.
risks: Channel relationships (distributors/contractors/utilities) could create some indirect network effects (preference and availability), but without disclosed active-participant counts over time (and without liquidity/share-of-wallet metrics) it is hard to verify true network-effect strength or acceleration.

Hubbell’s moat is more likely driven by product breadth, reliability, and channel execution; a well-funded competitor with similar distribution access could replicate distributor bundling/cross-sell programs, limiting durability of any network-effect claim.

evidence: Hubbell generated $5.0B (2022) to $5.8B (2025) in revenue with operating margin rising from 14.3% (2022) to 20.7% (2025), consistent with scale-related cost discipline and operating leverage despite modest top-line growth (revenue CAGR 5.7%).

Cost structure shows improving productivity/cost management at scale: in 2023, Hubbell reduced cost of goods sold as a % of net sales by 540 bps to 64.9% vs. 70.3% in 2022, lifting gross profit margin to 35.1% vs. 29.7% in 2022; in 2024, management attributed operating margin expansion to favorable price realization, productivity, and cost management (while noting partial offset from cost inflation and lower volume).

Selling & administrative intensity is meaningfully improved at larger scale: S&A expense as a % of net sales increased to 15.8% in 2023 from 2022 levels, but the company reported 2024 S&A of $812.5M on $5.6285B net sales (~14.4%), indicating a lower overhead burden than 2023; this is consistent with scale absorption even as the company executes portfolio changes (residential lighting exit in 2024).

Scale shows up in free cash conversion: free cash flow margin increased from 9.2% (2022) to 15.0% (2025), supporting that Hubbell’s size and operating margin expansion are translating into durable cash economics rather than one-off accounting effects.

Hubbell explicitly frames its strategy around delivering products with a 'competitive cost structure' and 'productivity and cost management,' and in 2024 it reported operating margin increase driven by favorable price realization, productivity and cost management (management-reported operating levers that typically benefit from scale-enabled manufacturing and procurement execution).
risks: Economies-of-scale proof versus true direct peers is indirect here: the web evidence collected supports internal margin/productivity drivers (price/cost/productivity) but does not quantify Hubbell’s unit-cost advantage (e.g., per-unit COGS) against similarly sized wiring/utility-component competitors.

Gross margin cyclicality is still evident: Hubbell reported that 2024 margin contraction drivers included material/other cost inflation and lower volume (partially offset by productivity and price), suggesting cost advantages may be vulnerable when inputs inflate or volumes soften.
Debt-to-equity of 128.87% (latest) can amplify earnings/cash volatility, potentially limiting the durability of any scale-based outperformance if financing costs rise or demand weakens.

bear_case: Hubbell’s 2024 gross profit margin fell to ~33.8%/33.9% (vs. ~35.1% in 2023) with the company attributing the decline to higher intangible amortization expense, higher material/other cost inflation, and lower unit volume—showing pricing power is not sufficient to fully defend margins when volumes soften.

Hubbell reported that the decrease in operating margin in 2024 included ~4 percentage points of margin contraction from material/other cost inflation plus higher acquisition-related intangible amortization and lower unit volume, partially offset by ~3 percentage points of favorable price realization and productivity/cost management—indicating margin is still meaningfully exposed to cost/volume pressures.
Hubbell continues to operate with high leverage (debt-to-equity reported ~128.9%), which can amplify downside risk to moat-driven economics if unit volume or realization weakens simultaneously.

Hubbell’s Electrical Solutions business shows evidence of demand/mix volatility tied to divestiture and volume: organic net sales were flat in 2024 because lower unit volume was offset by price realization (and 2024 net sales were also pressured by the residential lighting business disposition during Q1 2024), which weakens the case that brand/pricing power is independently driving steady economic moat outcomes.

stocks.investment_implication: Roper’s narrow, stable moat rests on customer loyalty and pricing power in its vertical software businesses, supported by network effects in platforms such as iPipeline. Its 6.2% return on invested capital provides weak confirmation despite stable operating margins near 28%, so the 5.9 rating is capped by financial evidence. The moat looks durable, though network effects are concentrated in only part of the portfolio.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Roper’s software customer relationships support recurring revenue, while operating margins remained between 28.2% and 28.4% from 2022 to 2025.
stocks.key_risk: Competition from well-capitalized rivals such as Uber Freight could weaken Roper’s DAT freight network and its pricing power.

evidence: Roper’s operating margin stayed remarkably steady at 28.4% (2022), 28.2% (2023), 28.4% (2024), and 28.3% (2025), indicating resilience consistent with pricing power rather than pure volume-led growth.
Roper’s gross margin remained very high and stable in the ~69% range across 2022–2025 (gross profit margin about 69.9% in 2022, 69.7% in 2023, 69.3% in 2024, and 69.2% in 2025).

Roper’s free-cash-flow (FCF) margin was elevated and strong versus earlier years—12.4% (2022), 31.2% (2023), 32.4% (2024), and 30.8% (2025)—supporting that pricing / mix has not been structurally eroding profitability.

Roper reported software-recurring portfolio durability: enterprise customer logo retention for software recurring revenue is in the mid-to-high 90s, and CEO commentary indicated blended enterprise net retention around the ~105% range (implying customers renew and expand rather than churn).

Roper indicated continued backlog/revenue-support for renewals: it expected to recognize revenues on ~63% of remaining performance obligations over the next 12 months, and backlog increased to $3,471.6 at September 30, 2026 from $3,174.0 at September 30, 2025 (evidence of demand durability for contracted software/renewal cycles).
risks: Roper is diversified across vertical application software and technology-enabled products, so brand/pricing-power metrics may vary materially by acquired business and vertical (pricing power may not be uniform across the portfolio).
Net retention and logo retention metrics are typically disclosed at the portfolio level; they may mask pockets of competitive pressure or churn risk in specific modules or customer segments.
While operating margin is stable, Roper’s latest-year ROIC is ~6.1% (latest year estimate), which suggests returns may not fully reflect a premium pricing moat at the consolidated level.

evidence: Roper’s disclosed capital intensity is low for a typical software company start-up but not negligible: in 2025 it reported total capital expenditures of $68.0 million and capitalized software expenditures of $40.0 million.

Roper’s business is built around “vertical software and technology-enabled product businesses,” implying that competitive differentiation is more execution/customer-specific than a single platform-scale monopoly; its latest SEC filing describes this diversified vertical-software model.

Roper reports additional technology/know-how embedded in acquired businesses via amortizable intangibles—its 2026 Form 10-Q disclosed amortizable technology of $33.0 million (6.4-year weighted average useful life) and customer relationships of $284.2 million (21.5-year weighted average useful life) related to acquisitions, indicating some IP/technology assets exist but with relatively limited residual life.

Roper has made ongoing acquisitions (e.g., 2025 acquisitions and notable 2024/2025 deals), which can help sustain defensibility by acquiring capabilities/installed bases, but it also means entry barriers are not solely organic and may be replicable by well-funded acquirers.
risks: The key dimension requested—patent portfolio size, key patents, and patent expiry timeline—could not be evidenced with concrete, company-specific patent-count and expiry data from accessible sources in this run; this limits confidence in scoring barriers derived from IP exclusivity.

Roper operates across multiple vertical software categories; without segment-level regulatory lock-in/licensing detail, the analysis cannot confirm whether there are meaningful license/regulatory barriers that would materially slow a new entrant from reaching feature/function parity.

evidence: Roper’s software revenue mix includes recurring and contract-linked streams: software and related services are categorized as (1) recurring (SaaS subscriptions and post-contract support (“PCS”) recognized ratably over the contractual term) and (2) non-recurring (perpetual or multi-year term licenses), which mechanically increases customer switching friction versus purely transactional software.

Roper reports that it has remaining performance obligations (“backlog”) that are expected to be recognized as revenue over time; at September 30, 2026 backlog increased to $3,471.6 million (with Application Software backlog of $2,598.5 million), indicating many customers have ongoing, contract-committed work/support that reduces near-term churn.

Roper discloses that SaaS subscriptions and PCS are recognized ratably over the contractual term, and that multi-year term license renewals and implementations can create contract-associated billing/unbilled receivables—both consistent with customers being on multi-period agreements rather than month-to-month terms.

Roper states it has a documented portfolio durability metric for software recurring revenue: “Gross logo retention of software recurring revenue,” with enterprise representing ~85% of software recurring revenue (excluding certain businesses). This suggests retention is a key operating KPI for the recurring install base, which is supportive of non-trivial switching costs.

However, Roper’s disclosed materials (including revenue recognition and backlog disclosures) do not provide customer-level churn/retention rates or explicit migration cost estimates (e.g., data export effort, re-integration costs, termination penalties), so the switching-cost impact is inferred from contract structure rather than directly quantified.
risks: If Roper’s recurring revenue is concentrated in contracts that are renewable but not meaningfully penalizing to exit (or if data/workflow portability is strong), then effective switching costs may be closer to “moderate” even if accounting indicates contract terms and backlog.

Roper’s software footprint is diversified across vertical products (Application Software, Network Software, Technology Enabled Products), so switching-cost intensity may vary widely by sub-business; without sub-segment churn and customer migration disclosures, the blended switching-cost rating may be misleading.

The retention evidence found is KPI-level (“gross logo retention”) without the actual retention/churn numbers, limiting the ability to score switching costs at the higher (7–8+) end where quantified retention implies strong lock-in.

evidence: Roper’s Network Software segment includes multiple platform-like businesses (e.g., DAT electronic marketplaces, ConstructConnect construction project network, iPipeline insurance distribution platform, and iTradeNetwork marketplaces), indicating that some Roper products become more valuable as connected participants use the shared workflow/data networks.

iPipeline (a Roper Network Software business) describes an ecosystem of “approximately 150 carriers,” “1,350 distributors,” and “over 500,000 agents,” implying direct and cross-side effects between insurers/carriers and downstream distribution participants.

Roper’s Network Software includes DAT, which Roper describes as serving brokers, carriers, owner-operators, and shippers, and as being “connected to more than 500,000 agents and advisers/advisors” (Roper page language), supporting a participant-count-based network effect for freight matching / related workflows.

At the portfolio level, Roper’s recurring revenue profile is substantial (consistent with software/platform lock-in), and Roper reported Network Software net revenues of $1,600.8 million in 2025 (20.3% of total net revenues), indicating that these network-exposed businesses are financially material to the company.

Roper’s reported financial performance from 2022–2025 shows strong top-line compounding (revenue rising from $5.4B to $7.9B; 13.7% CAGR per the provided figures) while operating margins stayed near ~28% (28.4% in 2022, ~28.2–28.4% in 2023–2025 per the provided figures), which is consistent with durable customer retention/renewal dynamics typical of network-enabled vertical software platforms (though it does not prove network effects specifically).
risks: Roper is a holding company spanning many vertical software and tech-enabled product businesses; only some sub-businesses are clear two-sided marketplaces/networks, so network effects may be concentrated rather than company-wide.

The web evidence found provides participant counts/connected ecosystem size for specific network businesses (e.g., iPipeline agents; DAT connected agents/advisers) but did not provide a consistent 3–5 year trend in those participant counts or marketplace liquidity metrics (e.g., transaction volumes, match rates, take rates) for Roper’s networks, limiting confidence in whether network effects are accelerating.

Competitors in the same vertical-network categories (e.g., insurance distribution platforms, construction preconstruction networks, freight marketplaces) may also grow their own participant bases, and the evidence gathered did not quantify whether Roper’s networks are gaining share vs. peers over the last 3–5 years.

evidence: Roper scaled revenue from $5.4B (2022) to $7.9B (2025) while keeping operating margin essentially flat at ~28.2%–28.4% from 2022–2025, indicating limited but real unit/economies-of-scale benefits showing up in cost discipline rather than expanding margins.

Cost structure shows scale-friendly operating leverage: selling, general & administrative expense as a percentage of net revenues decreased to 39.9% in 2024 vs. 41.2% in 2023, attributed to expense reductions and operating leverage on higher organic revenues (implying costs grow slower than revenue during higher-demand periods).

Gross margin profile supports scale-maintained economics: Roper reported gross margin decreased to 68.4% in 2024 vs. 68.9% in 2023 due primarily to acquisition mix (higher-margin mix dilution from acquisition payments revenue mix), not a deterioration in underlying cost structure—suggesting scale has not been overwhelmed by higher costs.

Roper’s absolute cost base grows with scale (cost of sales $2.16B in 2024 on $7.04B net revenues; cost of sales $2.43B in 2025 on $7.90B net revenues), but operating profit increased from $1.997B (2024) to $2.235B (2025), indicating that incremental revenue is being converted without a proportional rise in operating cost burden.
risks: Economies-of-scale risk: operating margin is flat (~28.3%–28.4%) rather than expanding, so scale benefits appear more like stable cost discipline than a widening cost gap vs competitors.

Supply-chain/procurement scale is not clearly evidenced for Roper’s software-heavy model: available filings emphasize expense rationalization and organic operating leverage, but do not provide direct unit-cost or bulk-purchasing/supplier-exclusivity metrics that would prove structural procurement advantages.

bear_case: Roper’s consolidated return profile shows weak capital efficiency versus a typical “premium moat” expectation: trailing ROIC is ~6.1% in the latest year estimate despite mid-to-high 28% operating margins (2022–2025 operating margin ~28.2%–28.4%).

Roper completed multiple material acquisitions in 2025 (including Subsplash and Convoy), and its margin commentary attributes gross margin softness to mix from these acquisitions (e.g., “payments revenue mix at Subsplash”), indicating the quality/strength of profitability is not uniformly moat-driven across the portfolio.

Competition/substitution pressure exists in at least one major network-enabled vertical: Roper’s freight-matching exposure (DAT/Convoy) faces large, well-capitalized digital freight competitors such as Uber Freight, as described in freight-matching industry coverage that frames DAT/Truckstop as critical players amid broker/digital marketplace competition.

Roper’s switching-cost and network-effect strengths are only indirectly evidenced: disclosed backlog and recurring revenue recognition describe contractual structure, but the company does not disclose customer churn/migration metrics to quantify whether exit costs are high enough to justify a high switching-cost score across the full software portfolio.

Operating margin positive in every year.

stocks.investment_implication: T. Rowe Price’s narrow, stable moat rests on its brand and retirement-plan relationships, though network benefits are limited in its core asset-management business. Approximate return on invested capital of 24.4% and return on equity of 18.2% support the moat, but $43.2 billion in 2024 net outflows and declining fees temper its durability.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: T. Rowe Price reported 97% retirement-plan client retention in 2023, supporting its brand strength despite firmwide outflows.
stocks.key_risk: Continued client outflows and shifts toward lower-fee products could erode revenue and margins, weakening the moat.

evidence: T. Rowe Price’s operating margin remained high but volatile over the last 4 fiscal years: 38.5% (2022) → 31.5% (2023) → 34.9% (2024) → 33.9% (2025).

Investment-advisory pricing (annualized effective fee rate, excluding performance-based fees) was essentially flat to slightly down: 41.9 bps (2023) → 41.0 bps (2024), based on the firm’s disclosed average annualized effective fee rate.
Profitability indicates some pricing power/brand strength through margins: net margin increased from 24.0% (2022) to 27.7% (2023) and 29.6% (2024), then remained elevated at 28.5% (2025).
Client/asset retention is a key brand-loyalty proxy in retirement services: T. Rowe Price states a 97% client retention rate (2023 and average over 2021–2023) for its retirement plan services.
However, the firm still reported substantial net outflows in 2024, signaling that loyalty/pricing power is not “near-zero churn”: net client outflows were $43.2B for 2024.
risks: Net outflows (e.g., $43.2B for 2024) imply that even with strong service branding, competitive pricing and/or investment-performance sensitivity can drive customer behavior and constrain pricing power.

Annualized effective fee rate excluding performance-based fees declined modestly from 41.9 bps (2023) to 41.0 bps (2024), suggesting pricing power can erode via mix shifts toward lower-fee products/classes.
AUM flows and effective fee rates are cyclical with markets; if AUM shifts accelerate, operating leverage could reverse even if brand remains strong.

evidence: T. Rowe Price discloses licensed and portfolio-related patents on its corporate “Intellectual Property” page, including U.S. Patent No. 8712808 and related licensed U.S. patents such as 5,128,984; 5,828,734; 5,684,863; 5,815,551; 5,974,120; and 5,898,762 (the page does not provide a complete patent count or a clear expiry schedule).

The firm is subject to Investment Advisers Act of 1940 registration and substantive regulatory requirements for its investment-advisory subsidiaries (including fiduciary duties, conflicts management, compliance programs, recordkeeping, reporting, and disclosure), which creates baseline compliance friction for entrants but is not a sector-wide exclusive license monopoly.

T. Rowe Price capitalizes material internal technology/software development costs: it capitalized $182.0 million of computer software for internal use in 2024 ($156.1 million in 2023; $134.6 million in 2022).

T. Rowe Price’s 2024 Annual Report shows a large technology/infrastructure spend: it increased “property and equipment expenditures” by $115.5 million in 2024, and it also discloses additional “capitalized” internal labor for software development (indicating sustained ongoing investment rather than one-time set-up costs).

Entry and scale in its core product model is supported by seed capital: at December 31, 2024, T. Rowe Price had seed capital investments of $1.3 billion in sponsored products, and it generally seeds new products to build performance history before relying on sustainable external assets—raising the financial runway required for an entrant to compete in product track record creation.
risks: The disclosed IP evidence is qualitative (specific patent numbers are listed) and does not provide an aggregate patent portfolio size or an expiry/timeline; if the real patent protection is limited or not central to its investment process, barriers from IP could be overstated.

Asset management is highly regulated but competition is not structurally blocked by licensing exclusivity (many entrants can register as investment advisers and build offerings), so regulatory compliance may be a cost/effort barrier rather than a durable moat.

evidence: T. Rowe Price’s disclosed investor-facing brokerage-account transfer process indicates migration is operationally non-trivial but feasible: T. Rowe Price “generally processes transfer requests the same day” and “most brokerage account transfers normally take approximately two weeks,” while “mutual fund transfers typically take two to three weeks,” implying material but not prohibitive time cost when switching custodians/transfer agents.

T. Rowe Price states it charges limited explicit transfer friction: it “will not charge a fee to transfer assets unless a foreign security fee applies,” and it describes an outgoing/inbound custody/DRS-related fee context including “DRS fee of $15.00” when book-entry positions are moved into a T. Rowe Price brokerage account, indicating switching is generally not monetarily penalized by T. Rowe Price itself (beyond specific edge cases).

T. Rowe Price’s own performance/fee disclosures show assets can move across strategies/products via “client flows and transfers,” with the company stating that its 2025 effective fee rate declined from 2024 “primarily due to client flows and transfers shifting assets under management toward lower-fee strategies and products,” suggesting investors can reallocate within/away from higher-fee offerings rather than being locked in by proprietary formats alone.

T. Rowe Price reports ongoing net client outflows at the firm level, indicating churn occurs and assets can leave: in 2024, net flows were -$43.2B and in Q4 2024 net flows were -$19.3B (management materials/Earnings Release Supplement), which is inconsistent with extremely high switching costs that would keep AUM/sticky retention steadily positive.
risks: Switching costs in asset management can be dominated by contract terms and plan/custodian rules (e.g., retirement-plan/recordkeeping constraints, minimum advisory relationships, wrap or share-class lockups); available evidence here is largely about account transfers and outflows rather than explicit multi-year termination penalties for discretionary advisory mandates.

AUM outflows do not identify the specific mechanics of switching (full account transfers vs. marginal reallocations, in-kind vs. liquidation, or advisor-driven moves); without client-level churn/retention metrics, the inferred migration cost remains partially indirect.

evidence: T. Rowe Price’s “full-service recordkeeping and plan administration” business provides cross-side-like network value through large, sticky retirement relationships: it served over 8,000 U.S. retirement plans and over 2.3 million plan participants (assets under administration of $282B as of December 31, 2024).

Participant base growth appears to be incremental rather than explosive: full-service recordkeeping participants were about 2.3M at December 31, 2024, and about 2.4M plan participants was disclosed for March 31, 2025 (recordkeeping AUA ~$280B as of March 31, 2025), indicating modest scale expansion with some volatility in AUA/flows rather than accelerating user growth.

Firmwide AUM level support is consistent with installed-base reinforcement: total AUM increased from $1,274.7B at December 31, 2023 to $1,606.6B at December 31, 2024 (SEC supplement shows AUM by period).

Network reinforcement is present but not clearly a direct “more users → higher monetization per incremental user” dynamic: T. Rowe Price reported net client outflows of $81.8B in 2023 versus $43.2B in 2024 (annual report/earnings release), implying the installed base is resilient, but the business is not showing accelerating inflow-driven network effects during the last two years.
risks: In core asset management, direct network effects are weak because investing value for existing clients typically does not increase materially just because more investors join (performance, distribution, and product design matter more than “platform adoption”).

Recordkeeping/plan relationships can be competed away: 401(k) recordkeeping market-share is concentrated among large incumbents (e.g., Fidelity and others), and recordkeeper switching remains costly but feasible for plan sponsors—so the network benefit is not winner-take-all for T. Rowe Price.

evidence: T. Rowe Price generated $6.5B of revenue in both 2022 and 2023, then increased to $7.1B in 2024 and $7.3B in 2025, indicating it can scale revenue with only modest top-line expansion over the last several years ($6.5B → $7.3B).

Operating leverage is mixed but generally positive: operating margin was 38.5% (2022) and 31.5% (2023), then improved to 34.9% (2024) and 33.9% (2025), while revenue rose from $6.5B (2023) to $7.1B (2024) and $7.3B (2025).

Cost structure suggests some economies of scale, but not ever-expanding: free cash flow margin fell sharply from 32.7% (2022) to 14.1% (2023) before recovering to 17.8% (2024) and 20.2% (2025), implying scale benefits are not consistently translating into expanding cash generation per dollar of revenue.

Revenue growth outpaced operating expense growth at least in 2024: operating expenses were $4,760.3M in 2024 (+6.4% vs 2023), while revenue was $7.1B in 2024 (+~9.1% vs 2023 at $6.5B), consistent with partial operating leverage from higher average AUM.

Scale is visible in business economics: firmwide AUM was $1.61T as of December 31, 2024, and average AUM in 2024 was $1.56T; the company’s operating model earns investment advisory revenues over $6.4B in 2024, supporting substantial fixed-cost absorption typical of larger asset managers.
risks: Operating margin is not steadily expanding over 2022–2025 (38.5% → 31.5% → 34.9% → 33.9%), which weakens the case that economies of scale are persistently widening the cost gap versus other large asset managers.

Fee-rate pressure and product mix can offset scale-driven cost absorption: the company notes annualized effective fee rates can be impacted by shifts toward lower-fee products/classes and tiered-fee structures, which can dilute any unit-cost advantages from larger AUM.

Free cash flow margin is volatile (32.7% in 2022 vs 14.1% in 2023), suggesting that even if the cost base benefits from scale, cash conversion may be affected by working-capital/capital-market dynamics or other non-cost factors that competitors can also navigate.

bear_case: T. Rowe Price reported full-year 2024 net client outflows of $43.2 billion and Q4 2024 net client outflows of $19.3 billion, indicating assets and clients are still leaving at a material pace despite the company’s stated retention efforts.

T. Rowe Price’s investment-advisory annualized effective fee rate (excluding performance-based fees) declined to 41.0 bps in 2024 from 41.9 bps in 2023, consistent with fee-rate pressure/mix shift away from higher-fee outcomes rather than clean pricing power.

Operating margin materially weakened versus 2022 after clients/fees pressured the revenue base: operating margin fell from 38.5% (2022) to 31.5% (2023) before only partially recovering to 34.9% (2024) and 33.9% (2025), showing the moat is not producing steadily expanding profitability.

Free cash flow margin was highly unstable—dropping from 32.7% (2022) to 14.1% (2023) before recovering to 17.8% (2024) and 20.2% (2025)—suggesting moat economics are not consistently translating into durable cash-generation power.

Net margin positive in every year.

stocks.investment_implication: FactSet’s wide, stable moat rests on customer loyalty and pricing power, reinforced by the difficulty of replacing its embedded data and workflow tools. Approximate return on invested capital of 17.8% and return on equity of 25.5% support the assessment, while annual subscription value retention above 95% points to durability despite recent margin pressure.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: FactSet’s annual subscription value retention above 95% and reported price increases show customers’ willingness to renew and pay for its services.
stocks.key_risk: Rising service costs and competition could erode pricing power and profitability, as reflected in the operating margin decline from 32.2% in fiscal 2025 to 28.3% in fiscal 2026.

evidence: FactSet reports annual ASV (Annual Subscription Value) retention greater than 95% (and client retention of ~91% when expressed as a % of clients) as of August 31, 2025, indicating near-consistent renewal/retention over the last several years.

FactSet’s reported operating margin increased from 30.2% in fiscal 2023 to 31.8% in fiscal 2024, and its net margin increased from 22.4% (fiscal 2023) to 24.4% (fiscal 2024), consistent with sustained pricing power rather than commoditized pricing.
FactSet’s reported operating margin was 32.2% in fiscal 2025 (after 31.8% in fiscal 2024), showing margin resilience over the last 3 years, before declining to 28.3% in fiscal 2026.

FactSet indicates pricing strength specifically through its revenue driver language (e.g., for the period ended November 30, 2024, revenue increases were driven by demand and price increases primarily from workstations, CGS, and data solutions).
risks: Reported margins weakened in fiscal 2026 (operating margin down to 28.3% and net margin down to 21.5%), which could signal emerging pricing pressure or mix headwinds if sustained.

FactSet’s pricing power may face longer-run competitive substitution risk from alternative data/analytics platforms and bundled market-data offerings, especially if clients can standardize workflows more cheaply over time.

evidence: FactSet’s capitalized “Developed technology” (internal-use software costs) is sizable and amortized over short cycles (e.g., developed technology useful life typically 3–5 years), with ongoing additions: fiscal 2024 “developed technology” amortization/charges are referenced in its 10-K accounting for internally built software assets.

Reported investment level is material but not prohibitive: capital expenditures were $60.8 million in fiscal 2023 (driven by capitalization of compensation costs related to internal-use software, plus some data center/network equipment), as stated in FactSet’s filings.

FactSet also capitalizes software-related costs and holds multiple proprietary data/technology intangibles; its disclosures describe a “Developed technology” category that includes capitalized internal-use software and software acquired for internal use, indicating proprietary know-how embedded in product delivery.

Entry is constrained by the need to assemble and maintain access to many third-party market data/content sources at scale: FactSet’s business description emphasizes integrating data from numerous premier providers and notes that some datasets have limited suppliers, which increases sourcing friction for a new entrant.

FactSet reports scale of commercial footprint (e.g., in its FY2026 filing, “more than 9,200 clients” and “over 260,000 professionals using our solutions”), which makes matching distribution and workflow integration a non-trivial switching/rollout effort for new competitors even without regulatory licensing barriers.
risks: The most decisive barrier—durable exclusivity from patents with long remaining life—was not evidenced with specific patent counts, named key patents, or an expiry timeline from authoritative patent databases in the sourced materials; as a result, the IP/barrier score may be overstated relative to reality.

This barrier assessment likely underweights the practical moat from switching costs/contract structure and instead focuses on disclosed accounting categories (capitalized internal-use software and capex); if customer stickiness is even stronger than suggested by the evidence, the true barriers could be higher.

Despite high profitability and substantial ongoing R&D/technology investment, the presence of multiple data suppliers and the existence of other financial-data platforms mean a well-funded entrant can still compete; if competitors replicate workflows faster than implied, barriers would be weaker than the score assumes.

evidence: FactSet reported annual ASV retention greater than 95% and annual retention of ~90% by clients for the year ended August 31, 2026 (9,258 clients; 260,671 professionals using FactSet).
FactSet reported annual ASV retention greater than 95% and annual retention of approximately 90% by clients for the year ended August 31, 2024 (8,217 clients; 216,381 professionals using FactSet).

FactSet states that clients access its capabilities through software applications, data feeds and APIs, or managed services, and that clients often use multiple access forms simultaneously—indicating integration/workflow embedding that increases migration friction.

FactSet indicates the majority of its contracts provide access to its platforms over the contractual term (with revenues recognized over time as clients consume daily access benefits), consistent with subscription-style arrangements where switching away implies replacing an ongoing, embedded daily workflow.

FactSet disclosed that “most” of its customers are on three-year contracts and that those contracts have longer 90-day cancellation periods and “floors and ceilings,” which is consistent with contractual commitment and cancellation friction that can raise switching costs.
risks: FactSet’s public disclosures provide retention and broad contract-structure signals, but do not disclose specific, quantified customer migration costs (e.g., re-integration effort, data normalization costs, or contract termination fees) in the sources reviewed here.

Retention metrics (ASV and client counts) do not directly identify the counterfactual migration effort or price concessions required to win/switch specific customers, so switching-cost magnitude is inferred rather than explicitly measured.

The “three-year contracts / 90-day cancellation periods / floors and ceilings” evidence is from an external transcript source rather than a FactSet 10-K exhibit or a contract template disclosure, so contract terms should be treated as directional until corroborated in primary contract language.

evidence: FactSet’s usage-based network-like installed base grew materially: professionals using FactSet increased from 186,463 as of Feb 28, 2023 to 237,324 as of Aug 31, 2025 (up 50,861, ~27.3% over ~30 months).

Professionals continued to grow through 2023–2025 with broadly positive 12-month net additions (e.g., 189,972 as of Aug 31, 2023 vs. prior year +5.6%; 206,478 as of Feb 29, 2024 vs. prior year +10.7%; 220,496 as of May 31, 2025 vs. prior year +5.9%).

Retention/lock-in indicators remained very high—annual ASV retention was >95% in each of the most recent reported periods (e.g., >95% for year ended Aug 31, 2024 and >95% for year ended Aug 31, 2025), implying a compounding installed-base value that is hard to replace even as users expand.

FactSet’s client count also scaled alongside the user base: clients increased from 8,217 as of Aug 31, 2024 to 9,258 as of Aug 31, 2026 (net +1,041; ~12.7% over ~24 months), consistent with durable enterprise adoption of the platform workflow.

In its Fixed Income/market connectivity offering, LiquidityBook (part of FactSet) operates a proprietary FIX network with connectivity to “over 200 brokers” and routing to “more than 1,600 destinations across 80 markets,” which can create cross-side network value for workflow users dependent on counterpart connectivity.
risks: FactSet’s core value is primarily proprietary data, analytics, and workflow integration rather than a classic two-sided marketplace; cross-side network effects are narrower and largely concentrated in specific connectivity/workflow modules (e.g., LiquidityBook).

Competitive substitutes (other data/workstation providers and internal broker/wealth platforms) can reduce switching economics over time if feature/function parity improves, even though retention has been >95% on ASV.

evidence: FactSet’s revenue scaled from $2.1B (FY2023) to $2.5B (FY2026), while maintaining very high profitability with operating margin of 30.2% (FY2023), 31.8% (FY2024), 32.2% (FY2025) and 28.3% (FY2026), indicating broadly strong cost discipline as the business scales.

Cost structure shows scale-like operating leverage but not steadily improving: FY2024 and FY2025 saw operating margin expansion (31.8%→32.2%) alongside revenue rising from $2.2B to ~$2.3B, while FY2026 margin compressed to 28.3% despite revenue increasing to ~$2.5B, suggesting costs are not consistently “flowing through” with scale.

FactSet’s unit-cost proxy (cost of services as a share of revenue) rose in FY2026: cost of services was 49.4% of revenue in fiscal 2026, up 210 bps vs FY2025, implying that the marginal cost efficiency benefit of scale weakened over the last year.

Operating scale is supported by large client/user bases: FactSet reported 9,258 clients and 260,671 professionals using FactSet as of Aug 31, 2026 (up from 8,996 clients and 237,324 professionals as of Aug 31, 2025), consistent with the company spreading substantial fixed/semifixed platform and personnel costs across a larger footprint.

SG&A is relatively controlled versus revenue at scale and has been trending down: SG&A was 20.5% of revenues in fiscal 2025 (down 170 bps vs fiscal 2024), supporting the view that overhead does not scale one-for-one with revenue (a scale/economies-of-scale signal).
risks: FY2026 margin compression (operating margin 32.2% in FY2025 to 28.3% in FY2026) and higher cost-of-services ratio (49.4% of revenue in FY2026) weaken evidence that scale is currently widening the cost gap versus competitors.

FactSet’s business has meaningful variable cost components tied to delivering and updating data/content and services; if these costs rise faster than revenue, the economies-of-scale benefit can be offset (as suggested by the FY2026 cost-of-services increase).

bear_case: FactSet’s operating margin fell from 32.2% in fiscal 2025 to 28.3% in fiscal 2026, and net margin fell from 25.7% to 21.5%, indicating the economic moat is already being pressure-tested in reported results.

FactSet’s cost of services increased to 49.4% of revenue in fiscal 2026 (up 210 bps vs. fiscal 2025), consistent with margin compression from rising delivery/input costs rather than purely mix or one-time factors.

FactSet disclosed that revenue growth drivers included “workstations, CGS and data solutions” with revenue also partially offset by dispositions, implying that parts of the growth engine may be exposed to competitive demand/mix shifts that can pressure pricing and profitability.

FactSet is a named defendant in an antitrust case (CUSIP Global Services and FactSet) alleging conspiracy to eliminate competition in the use of a committee on uniform securities identification procedures, adding legal/regulatory overhang specifically tied to its market position.
