stocks.investment_implication: Prologis has a narrow, stable moat rooted in pricing power and tenant switching costs. Its latest approximate return on invested capital of 3.0% does not confirm strong returns, and weak financial evidence capped the rating despite consistently positive, stable operating margins. Long leases and customer retention support durability, but falling free cash flow margins temper confidence.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Prologis maintained operating margins near 38% from 2022 through 2025 and reported a 66.3% net effective rent change in 2024.
stocks.key_risk: Weak returns on invested capital threaten the moat’s value to investors, as Prologis’s latest approximate ROIC was only 3.0%.

evidence: Prologis’ operating margin was 38.2% (2022), 38.4% (2023), 37.8% (2024), and 38.8% (2025), indicating stable operating-level profitability consistent with durable differentiation rather than pure price-taking.

Prologis’ gross-margin proxy (reported as gross profit margin from third-party datasets) stayed high around the mid-to-high 70% range: 2022 ~74.7% and 2023 ~74.9%, and another dataset shows 2022/2023/2024 gross margin ~75.87%/75.95%/75.69%, suggesting no sustained margin compression over recent years.
Customer-satisfaction/brand perception evidence: Prologis was ranked 8th in customer satisfaction in The Wall Street Journal Management Top 250 (as reported by Nareit).

Brand value momentum (brand-valuation consultancy evidence): Brand Finance reported Prologis as the fastest-growing real estate brand in 2024 with +75.1% year-on-year brand value, reaching USD 1.7 billion.

Repeat/rental-renewal pricing power is indirectly supported by leasing/mark-to-market dynamics: Prologis reported lease mark-to-market of 29.2% (2022/2023 period shown in a hosted company dataset) and, for the FY2024 results package, disclosed a 'Net Effective Rent Change' of 66.3% along with 2024 'Cash Same Store NOI' of 6.7% (both consistent with ongoing positive rent/NOI outcomes rather than widespread discounting).
risks: Pricing-power durability is hard to isolate in a cyclical industrial REIT model: even with stable margins, Prologis’ latest ROIC is ~2.9% (latest-year approx.), which is not consistent with strong, continuously monetized pricing power translating into high incremental returns.

High leverage (debt-to-equity ~62.1%) can amplify the impact of leasing demand shocks and limit the ability to maintain favorable net pricing terms during downturns, increasing sensitivity to price competition.

evidence: Prologis’ scale and persistent reinvestment create capital-related barriers: in 2024 it disclosed “Strategic capital expenses” of $292 million and $385 million (net of strategic capital expense components shown in its 10-K table), while also reporting ongoing development/acquisition activity through its Real Estate and Strategic Capital segments.

Building and operating logistics real estate is explicitly constrained by permitting/entitlement and utility approvals: Prologis discloses risks that it may experience delays in obtaining “all necessary zoning, land-use, building, occupancy and other permits, authorizations and agreements,” including for “sufficient or reliable power for our data centers.”

Prologis operates at very large footprint, which raises the practical difficulty for a new entrant to reach “parity” quickly (time-to-scale barrier even if assets are not legally monopolized): as of Dec. 31, 2025, it reported >4,000 customers occupying 649 million square feet of logistics operating properties and 6,500 customers occupying 1.3 billion square feet for its O&M portfolio.

Prologis’ moat is not primarily patent-driven (no disclosed patent portfolio size/expiry schedule was found in the cited filings/results), implying barriers rely more on execution, site selection, and relationships than on enforceable IP: its 10-K emphasizes “proprietary technology and strategic partnerships” and customer experience teams via its Essentials platform rather than a quantified patent base.
risks: No quantified patent counts, key patent list, or expiry timeline for Prologis were located in the evidence gathered, so the company’s entry barriers from IP are not clearly evidenced here; this likely lowers the barriers score versus an IP-heavy business.

Industrial logistics REIT competition can emerge through land acquisition, development, and capital access (not a legal monopoly), so barriers may weaken if capital becomes cheaper or if local zoning constraints ease in key markets.

evidence: Prologis reports long-duration leasing: the weighted average term for leases commenced, including new leases and renewals, was 64 months in 2024.

Lease contract duration/expiration distribution implies limited near-term ability to churn space: Prologis’ 2024 operating portfolio shows a weighted average remaining lease term of 4.0 years (based on net effective rent).

Prologis discloses lease-lifecycle momentum via retention metrics, including Q2 2026 customer retention of 72.7% (retention defined by square footage of leases commenced during the period that are rented by existing tenants divided by square footage of expiring leases).
For 2024 (full year), Prologis reported a retention metric of 75.8% (same retention framework: square footage retained from expiring leases to leases commenced).

Operational and physical integration depth exists through facility customization and service offerings, including build-to-suit capabilities; Prologis specifically highlights development of logistics facilities tailored to customer needs (a key source of move/renovation cost when tenants relocate).
risks: Switching-cost magnitude is not clearly evidenced as costly/penalizing contract structures (e.g., early-termination fees, non-cancelable multi-year minimum commitments, or explicit proprietary data lock-in) in the sources captured; industrial REIT tenants can sometimes relocate within the same market if space is available.

Retention is high but does not directly quantify tenant-specific migration pain/cost (e.g., how much capex, time, or operational disruption a tenant incurs to move from one Prologis facility to another landlord).

evidence: Prologis serves an installed base of ~5,800 customers (2021) that increased to ~6,600 customers (2022) and ~6,700 customers (2023), then was ~6,500 customers in both 2024 and 2025 (as of 9/30/2025), indicating no sustained accelerating growth in “participants.”

Prologis’ operating customer concentration is significant at year-end 2024, with its top customer (Amazon) at ~6.0% of net effective rent (NER), and the top 10 customers totaling ~15.9% of NER (consolidated). This supports durable relationships but not a classic “more users make the product more valuable” marketplace dynamic.

Prologis reports an “O&M” scale of ~1.2B square feet at end-2022 (with ~6,600 customers) and ~1.3B square feet at 9/30/2025 (with ~6,500 customers), suggesting growth in owned/managed footprint rather than accelerating cross-side connectivity among participants.

Occupancy for the operating portfolio is consistently very high (e.g., ~95.6% average occupancy reported for 2024), indicating demand stability and customer stickiness, but it reflects lease/asset quality more than network effects where each added participant increases value to others.

Prologis explicitly frames its advantage around “depth of our customer relationships” and its platform capabilities (e.g., Customer Led Solutions/Prologis Essentials), but the evidence available here is relationship/asset-driven rather than participant-driven network effect reinforcement (e.g., no measurable two-sided marketplace liquidity metrics disclosed).
risks: If Prologis’ platform offerings (e.g., customer solutions/Prologis Essentials) drive measurable engagement or increasing tenant mix/value as the customer base grows, the network-effects score could be understated versus a “platform flywheel” interpretation.

Industrial REIT economics are not a pure marketplace model; competitors that share similar tenant stickiness could replicate “platform” capabilities, limiting true network effects durability over a 10-year horizon. (Network effects may be weak because the primary moat may be land/asset quality and execution rather than network.)

Competing logistics REITs/asset managers could narrow differentiation via development pipelines or customer service, and without explicit cross-side liquidity/metrics, it is hard to demonstrate that Prologis’ participant growth is structurally self-reinforcing.

evidence: Revenue scaled from $6.0B (2022) to $8.8B (2025), while operating margin stayed tightly range-bound at 38.2% (2022), 38.4% (2023), 37.8% (2024), and 38.8% (2025), indicating scale did not materially deteriorate cost structure.

Operating leverage signal is mixed on the headline cost line: net margin and free cash flow margin declined after 2022 (net margin 56.3% in 2022 vs 38.1% in 2023, 45.5% in 2024, 37.9% in 2025; FCF margin 69.1% in 2022 vs 57.0% in 2025), so scale benefits are present but not consistently widening into higher per-dollar profitability across the full cycle.

Scale in platform footprint is large: Prologis owned or invested in properties/development projects totaling ~1.3B square feet in 20 countries (as of March 31, 2026), supporting a broad operating footprint that typically enables standardized processes and procurement/logistics efficiencies at scale.

Funding/capital-structure scale appears to support financial flexibility (a key enabler of cost competitiveness in a REIT): Prologis reported unencumbered gross real estate assets to unsecured debt of 268.0% (Sept 30, 2026), plus investment-grade credit ratings (Moody’s A2, S&P A), which can help preserve access to capital for acquisitions/development versus smaller operators.

Scale translates into portfolio depth and operating continuity rather than materially higher operating margins: Prologis’ earnings release supplemental materials show large owned-and-managed operating portfolios with high occupancy (e.g., average occupancy ~95–97% across 2025 quarters shown in supplemental tables), implying scale helps sustain utilization (but still within an industry-typical margin band).
risks: Operating leverage evidence is not clearly strengthening over the last 3–5 years: despite revenue rising at a mid-teens CAGR, net margin and free cash flow margin both fell meaningfully versus 2022 levels, suggesting any cost-per-unit advantages may be competed away or offset by macro/transaction/valuation factors.

Economies of scale in industrial REITs may be less about lower GAAP cash operating costs per unit and more about property acquisition/development access and capital markets; this can make the “unit cost” moat harder to quantify versus more cost-structured businesses.

Return on invested capital is low in the latest year cited (~2.9%), implying that even if scale helps, it is not consistently producing high incremental economics that are structurally unmatched by other large industrial REITs.

bear_case: Prologis generated low returns on invested capital in its latest year cited (approx. ROIC ~2.9%), which is inconsistent with a strong, sustainably monetized moat even while operating margin stayed in a narrow band around ~38%.
Free cash flow margin declined materially from 69.1% (2022) to 57.0% (2025), indicating that whatever pricing/scale advantage exists did not translate into improving cash economics over time.

Prologis’ customer concentration remains meaningful (top customer Amazon at ~6.0% of net effective rent and top 10 customers at ~15.9% of NER), creating clear exposure to tenant decision risk rather than a broad-based network-like moat.

Prologis’ retention metrics, while still high (e.g., ~75.8% for 2024 and ~72.7% in Q2 2026), showed quarter-to-quarter deterioration rather than steady improvement, suggesting stickiness is not strengthening into an ever-stronger moat.

Operating margin positive in every year.

Free cash flow positive in every year.

stocks.investment_implication: PEG’s narrow, stable moat rests on regulatory barriers to entry and the scale of its New Jersey distribution network. Returns do not clearly confirm a strong moat: 2025 return on invested capital was 5.6%, and free cash flow margins were negative in 2022 and 2024. The rating is capped by this weak financial evidence, although the regulated franchise supports durability.
stocks.key_strength: High Barriers to Entry: PSE&G’s regulated delivery franchise and the capital required to replicate its infrastructure protect it from direct competition.
stocks.key_risk: Regulators could limit returns or recovery of PEG’s planned $22.5 billion to $26 billion in regulated capital spending for 2025–2029, weakening returns and cash flow.

evidence: Customer satisfaction evidence exists but is about experience/service rather than “repeat purchasing” or voluntary retention: PSE&G was ranked #1 in residential electric customer satisfaction in the East among large utilities in the J.D. Power 2025 U.S. Electric Utility Residential Customer Satisfaction Study, and PSEG Long Island scored 700 in that same study (2024 edition).

Pricing power is limited by regulation/pass-through mechanics: in PSE&G’s distribution model, PSE&G earns no margin on BGS/BGSS supply service because costs are passed back to customers; therefore, brand-driven pricing power (beyond authorized returns in distribution) is structurally constrained.

Margin durability shows volatility rather than consistent expansion: operating margin was 15.1% (2022) and surged to 32.8% (2023) but then fell to 22.9% (2024) and rose slightly to 24.5% (2025), indicating no steady multi-year gross/profit expansion profile.

Free cash flow margin is highly inconsistent, suggesting limited resilience of economic “pricing power”/self-funding beyond regulatory timing: -14.1% (2022), 4.3% (2023), -12.1% (2024), and 0.2% (2025).

Regulated bill increases were still material, implying customers faced higher prices rather than PSEG charging a persistent premium over alternatives: PSE&G’s electric+gas base rate settlement approved by the NJ BPU (announced Sep 9, 2024) indicated a typical combined residential electric and gas customer bill increase of ~7% (~$15/month), with some offsets from approved rate changes.
risks: Brand loyalty may not translate to durable pricing power because retail electricity/gas procurement is largely regulated and includes significant pass-throughs; thus “brand” may reflect service quality rather than willingness to pay a premium.

Regulatory outcomes and timing (rate case approvals, ROE allowed, storm cost recovery, and deferrals/flowbacks) can drive operating margin and cash flow materially, masking any underlying pricing power.

Economic moat durability could be pressured if service-quality performance deteriorates (customer satisfaction and service-level metrics) or if regulators reduce allowed returns, compressing margins despite any brand strength.

evidence: PSEG’s regulated electric transmission/distribution business is insulated from retail customer competition in its New Jersey service territory because it earns returns on its rate base for wires-and-pipes service (not commodity supply), and its base rates have been most recently approved in October 2024, with additional clause recovery mechanisms subject to prudency reviews by the NJ BPU.

PSEG is required to continuously secure/maintain major regulatory approvals for capital and rate recovery: its proposed projects may not be fully approved, and its capital investments can be lower than planned if regulators do not approve filings as requested.

Capital intensity is high enough to deter entrants: PSEG disclosed that its 2025–2029 regulated capital spending plan is $22.5 billion to $26 billion, and it initiated guidance showing ~$3.8 billion of regulated capital spending for 2025 (further supporting the scale/capex needed to compete for regulated rate-base growth).

PSEG’s nuclear generation has a regulatory life constraint and durability barrier: PSEG Nuclear LLC operates Hope Creek, and PSEG’s own corporate disclosure states the Hope Creek operating license was renewed until 2046 (a major long-lived asset that is difficult for entrants to replicate within a short timeframe).

Regulatory/market-rule evolution is still a competitive pressure but not a near-term eroder: PSEG states that prior FERC/PJM changes removed a prior “right of first refusal” to construct transmission projects in its service territory, implying third-party transmission construction can occur, but PSEG remains a transmission/distribution rate-base earner subject to ongoing tariff/formula mechanisms.
risks: Patent/IP barrier evidence is weak for this company specifically: publicly accessible sources did not provide a credible, company-specific patent count/key patent list and expiry timeline comparable to the regulatory and capital barriers, so the score is driven mainly by regulation and capital rather than proprietary IP.

If regulatory reforms substantially accelerate non-utility build/entry into transmission or reduce the recoverability of PSEG’s investment programs (e.g., changes to incentives/returns or restrictions on utility participation in certain areas), the practical time-to-parity for entrants could shorten and lower the barrier strength.

High leverage (debt-to-equity ~148.4%) can impair a potential entrant’s ability to fund the required regulatory capital program; conversely for PSEG itself, it increases financing risk that could affect willingness/ability to maintain the investment cadence regulators expect.

evidence: PSE&G’s retail electric and gas bills in New Jersey separate “delivery” (distribution utility) from “supply” (electric/gas supplier), and New Jersey policy allows customers to “shop” for electric and/or natural gas supply from third-party suppliers rather than the local utility company.

PSE&G states that a customer can switch energy suppliers and can “switch back to [their] regular service from PSE&G at any time,” indicating low practical switching friction for the supply component (as opposed to distribution service tied to territory).

New Jersey’s BPU switching materials describe that customers have the ability to choose third-party supply rather than the local utility for both electric and natural gas (a structural condition that limits customer lock-in).

PSE&G’s smart-meter (AMI) program involved large utility capital commitments and regulatory treatment for stranded/non-AMI legacy meter costs, with an order/discussion reflecting ~$714 million of investment over five years and stranded costs (e.g., non-AMI legacy meters removed). This supports technical/asset-specific lock-in, but it is a distribution-system infrastructure story rather than a clear “customer can’t switch” barrier for retail supply.

PSEG’s regulated utility financials do not show a customer-retention-based switching cost effect (e.g., no disclosed customer churn/retention metric in the sourced materials), while retail switching for the supply component is explicitly permitted and described as reversible by the company.
risks: Switching costs for PSEG may be understated by the available evidence because the most durable lock-in for the utility is typically distribution-service territory and operational integration, not retail “supply” choice; the sourced materials focus more on customer choice for supply than on customer inability to migrate distribution service.

The AMI/stranded-cost evidence shows significant migration costs for PSE&G’s infrastructure modernization, but it does not directly quantify the incremental cost/time for a *customer* to leave PSE&G’s service (vs. switching suppliers for the supply portion).

evidence: PSEG’s regulated electric distribution franchise is delivered via a fixed service territory; PSE&G provides distribution service to 2.4 million electric customers and 1.9 million gas customers across ~2,600 square miles in New Jersey (i.e., value is not increased by additional users on a two-sided marketplace basis).

PSE&G customer growth is low and rate-based rather than network-driven: PSEG reports 5-year annual customer growth of 0.9% for electric customers and 0.7% for gas customers (using 2019 as the base year).

PSEG’s value creation is primarily regulated T&D economics (tariffs/rate base) rather than platform liquidity: PSE&G’s rate base is ~ $34B for YE 2024, with distribution ~ $19.1B and transmission ~ $13.3B, which indicates the moat is infrastructure/regulation rather than participant-driven network effects.

PSEG’s customer base is largely “one-to-many” service provisioning (utilities deliver electricity/gas to end-users) and does not show cross-side participant aggregation metrics; the company does not present any buyer–seller marketplace liquidity or share-of-wallet metrics in its core customer data materials.

Competitive pressure exists via distributed energy resources and other retail/energy choices (which can affect load growth), but PSEG’s regulated T&D footprint remains effectively insulated from direct retail competition in the delivery franchise, which weakens the case for winner-take-most network effects.
risks: If PSEG’s non-regulated customer-energy services (e.g., appliance service provider, energy efficiency/renewable programs) exhibit measurable participant virality or partner-seller aggregation, network effects could be stronger than indicated by regulated customer counts alone.

The network-effects thesis could be under-measured because PSEG’s reported disclosures emphasize tariff/rate-base economics; network metrics (e.g., program enrollment loops, partner ecosystem density) may not be disclosed in the sources retrieved.

evidence: PSEG’s scale is reflected in its large regulated footprint: PSE&G provides distribution service to about 2.4 million electric customers and 1.9 million gas customers over ~2,600 square miles in New Jersey.

Operating leverage consistent with scale benefits: operating margin is positive and relatively strong across the period (15.1% in 2022, 32.8% in 2023, 22.9% in 2024, 24.5% in 2025) alongside revenue that rose overall from $9.8B (2022) to $12.2B (2025), implying costs did not rise proportionally to revenue for most years in the 2022–2025 window.

However, the scale advantage is not consistently visible in cash efficiency: free cash flow margin was negative in 2022 (-14.1%) and 2024 (-12.1%), turned positive in 2023 (4.3%) and slightly positive in 2025 (0.2%), suggesting that scale-driven profitability does not reliably translate into free-cash generation year-to-year.

Scale supports underpinnings for cost control in regulated operations: PSEG discloses a multi-year regulated capital investment program driving predictable regulated rate base growth (capex outlook described as leading to regulated rate base CAGR in a stated range of ~6% to ~7.5% from year-end 2024 to year-end 2029), which generally enables averaging of fixed costs and sustained execution scale, though this is investment-driven rather than direct unit-cost disclosure.

Cost-concentrated procurement/supply-chain scale is not directly evidenced with quantified 'unit cost per kWh' comparisons in the available filings/secondary sources, but PSEG’s business mix is large enough to support centralized functions (PSEG is the parent of PSE&G, PSEG Power, and other operating entities), with consolidation-level operating results showing persistent profitability (net margin 10.5% in 2022 and 17.3% in 2025).
risks: Regulated utility economics limit the ability to 'undercut' rivals on unit cost: many cost items (capital, O&M, storm costs, depreciation) are passed through or amortized subject to regulation, so economies of scale may not produce durable absolute cost leadership versus other large regulated utilities.

Free cash flow margin volatility (negative in 2022 and 2024) weakens the evidence that scale is converting into superior cost/working-capital economics rather than shifting capital timing and rate-regulatory cash flows.

The analysis lacks direct, company-specific unit-cost metrics (e.g., O&M per customer, cost per kWh, or delivered energy distribution cost) versus peer utilities, so the economies-of-scale score is based more on profitability/operating leverage and customer footprint than on measured unit-cost leadership.

bear_case: PSE&G’s commodity “supply” portion is structurally exposed to customer choice because New Jersey allows customers to “shop for energy suppliers” and PSE&G notes customers can switch energy suppliers and can switch back to PSE&G at any time, undermining durable pricing power in the area where customers most directly respond to prices.

Operating margin is volatile rather than consistently improving, falling from 32.8% (2023) to 22.9% (2024) before only modestly recovering to 24.5% (2025), which suggests moat returns are being pressured by execution/regulatory dynamics instead of compounding steadily.

Free cash flow margin shows repeated negative-to-low outcomes (-14.1% in 2022, 4.3% in 2023, -12.1% in 2024, 0.2% in 2025), indicating limited resilience/cash generation consistency that is inconsistent with a strongly entrenched economic moat.

PSEG faces nuclear life-cycle constraints that act like a timing headwind rather than a permanent moat shield: its nuclear strategy depends on license renewals and related regulatory processes (e.g., NRC subsequent license renewal intentions/renewal timelines), meaning a credible portion of value depends on regulatory outcomes.

reasons: Return on invested capital 5.6%.
Operating margin positive in every year.
Operating margin rose across the period and ended near its high.
Free cash flow negative or missing in at least one year.

stocks.investment_implication: Public Storage’s narrow moat, rated 5.9, rests on its operating scale and ability to raise rents for existing tenants. Its 8.3% return on invested capital and consistently positive operating margins and free cash flow provide adequate, though not conclusive, financial support. The moat is eroding: operating margin fell from 51.9% in 2022 to 46.9% in 2025, while new-tenant rates faced pressure.
stocks.key_strength: Economies of Scale: Public Storage’s 3,073 facilities across 40 states give it a large operating footprint, supporting strong profitability.
stocks.key_risk: Pressure on new-tenant rents threatens pricing power, with average rates per square foot charged to new tenants falling 11.6% in 2024.

evidence: Public Storage’s profitability has been strong but has deteriorated since 2022: operating margin fell from 51.9% (2022) to 46.9% (2024 and 2025), indicating some loss of pricing/margin power over the last 3 years.

Gross-margin performance is still high in recent reporting, but it has been pressured versus peak levels: Public Storage reported gross margin (before indirect costs, depreciation and amortization expense) of 78.5% (2023), 78.2% (2024), and 78.4% (2025) in its 2024/2025 results disclosures, showing slight erosion rather than expansion.

Public Storage’s disclosed same-store pricing shows rate increases but also occupancy headwinds, implying pricing is not fully offsetting demand: 2025 performance commentary states that the increase in realized annual rent per occupied square foot was driven by cumulative rate increases to existing long-term tenants over the past twelve months, partially offset by lower average rates for new move-ins.

Customer churn is meaningfully non-zero (which limits a 'near-zero churn' pricing-power rating): a recent Public Storage filing shows Same Store Churn of 18.2% versus 19.6% for the comparable period (with additional churn figures shown for other segments/time windows in the same filing).
risks: Operating margin compression from 51.9% (2022) to 46.9% (2024–2025) suggests pricing power may be weakening as the self-storage market absorbs demand/supply changes or promotional intensity rises.
Churn remains material (high-teens % in latest reported same-store measures), so premium pricing may be increasingly contested at the tenant level, especially for new move-ins.

evidence: Public Storage has a large, geographically distributed footprint: at December 31, 2024 it had controlling ownership interests in 3,073 self-storage facilities in 40 states, which raises scale and operational know-how but is not the same as IP- or regulatory-driven exclusivity.

Capital intensity for incremental growth is meaningful but not prohibitive in absolute terms: in 2024 Public Storage completed development/redevelopment activities costing $343.4 million and also completed the acquisition of 22 facilities for $267.5 million in cash, while it had facilities in development expected to add 2.5 million net rentable square feet at an estimated $498.9 million and expansion projects expected to add 1.5 million net rentable square feet at an estimated $242.7 million.

Ongoing maintenance CAPEX is recurring (i.e., entrants must also fund similar ongoing facility upkeep if they build/acquire): Public Storage reported ‘capital expenditures to maintain real estate facilities’ of $205.2 million (2022), $232.0 million (2023), and $234.5 million (2024).

The USPTO-linked evidence found for ‘Public Storage’ appears dominated by branding/trademark-style records rather than a clear, enforceable large-count utility patent portfolio for storage operations; for example, one listing shows many trademark entries (e.g., multiple ‘PS PUBLIC STORAGE…’ and ‘PUBLIC STORAGE ADVANTAGE…’ marks) rather than an identifiable set of technology patents that would materially slow a new entrant.

Public Storage’s ‘moat’ appears more acquisition-and-development scale-based than regulatory locked-in: it is actively acquiring and developing—since the beginning of 2022 it acquired 260 facilities with 18.5 million net rentable square feet for $3.7 billion and during 2023 it acquired the Simply portfolio (127 facilities; 9.4 million net rentable square feet) for $2.2 billion—suggesting barriers are primarily capital/land-development execution rather than licensing.
risks: Utility patent barriers may be understated by the available patent-record search result; if Public Storage has a substantial enforceable utility patent portfolio (not captured in the trademark-heavy evidence), the true entry barrier could be higher.

Regulatory/permit complexity for self-storage (zoning, building codes, fire/safety, environmental constraints) is not quantified here at the company/portfolio level; if Public Storage has unique permitting advantages in key jurisdictions, barriers could be stronger than this score.

The analysis focuses on entry barriers; Public Storage’s high margins could indicate operational advantages (pricing/occupancy know-how) that indirectly increase the time/cost for entrants to match economics, but this is not a quantified barrier metric in the sourced evidence.

evidence: Public Storage states its storage rentals are month-to-month agreements (not locked into long-term contracts), reducing contractual switching friction for customers.

Public Storage reports the same-store churn metric (units moved out during the period divided by starting occupied units); for the three months ended June 30, 2026, same-store churn was 18.2% (19.6% in the prior-year quarter), and for the six months ended June 30, 2026, same-store churn was 36.1% (38.9% prior-year).

Public Storage reports that in 2025 it generated revenue from existing long-term tenants and notes “more than half of our tenants have rented their space for longer than a year at December 31, 2025,” indicating retention is meaningful but not driven by long-term lease lock-in.

Public Storage reports that contract rents gained from move-ins and contract rents lost from move-outs are tracked annually in its filings, implying customers regularly leave and re-enter the customer base (i.e., movement between properties is an ongoing behavior rather than rare due to switching penalties).
risks: Self-storage customers may face some practical relocation costs (packing, driving, temporary storage) even if leases are month-to-month; the filings and cited customer-facing materials do not quantify these migration costs in dollars for PSA specifically.

While PSA’s churn figures show frequent customer moves, the data does not directly isolate the share attributable to switching versus space no longer needed; without this decomposition, the switching-cost component could be overstated or understated.

evidence: Public Storage had an installed base of 3,073 consolidated self-storage facilities (221.3 million net rentable square feet) operating under the Public Storage name at December 31, 2024, but this scale is not presented as a direct “more users → higher value” network effect; it primarily reflects asset ownership and operational scale rather than user-driven platform value.

Public Storage shows user-like digitization that could reinforce stickiness, including an eRental platform where online, contactless eRental leases accounted for ~60% of move-ins versus ~30% for peers (per the company’s proxy filing language), which supports operational preference/retention rather than measurable cross-side marketplace network effects.

Public Storage reports 1.4 million certificates of insurance held by participating self-storage customers at December 31, 2024 (aggregate coverage of ~$6.8 billion), indicating a customer-participant base that can reinforce ancillary revenues, but it does not evidence a bidirectional buyer–seller liquidity flywheel typical of stronger network effects.

Public Storage’s third-party management platform expanded to 402 properties in 2024 (133 properties added in 2024), suggesting a brand/operations distribution advantage that may be reinforced by partner experiences; however, the disclosures characterize this as brand/platform benefits to partners rather than a clear marketplace liquidity effect that strengthens with more users/customers.

Public Storage app downloads were reported at over 4.5 million with a 4.6/5.0 Apple rating in 2023 proxy disclosures, supporting digital engagement, but there is no company-provided metric showing that larger app adoption causally drives accelerating tenant move-in growth via platform liquidity.
risks: Self-storage is fundamentally a physical capacity business (facility-level supply/demand), so network effects that depend on increasing value with additional participants are hard to establish versus advantages from scale, location density, and pricing/operations.

Public Storage’s disclosed “participants” (insurance certificates, app downloads, move-in mix) support customer engagement and ancillary revenue, but the evidence provided does not demonstrate measurable cross-side liquidity or winner-take-most dynamics against other self-storage networks.

evidence: Public Storage grew from $4.2B of revenue (2022) to $4.8B (2025) and shows no major margin compression at the operating level: operating margin was 51.9% (2022), 51.3% (2023), and 46.9% in both 2024 and 2025. (Yahoo Finance figures as provided by user; corroborating 2024/2025 revenue and major expense lines appear in PSA’s filings.)

Operating leverage is weaker than a classic “scale widening the cost gap” story: while revenue rose, operating margin declined from ~51% (2022–2023) to 46.9% (2024–2025), suggesting costs rose roughly in line with (or faster than) revenues rather than being meaningfully levered down.

Scale is evident in physical footprint and national coverage: PSA had controlling interests in 3,073 self-storage facilities across 40 states in the U.S. as of December 31, 2024, with 221 million net rentable square feet under the Public Storage name.

PSA’s cost structure shows high operating profitability consistent with competitive advantages at scale (even if not clearly improving recently): 2025 total revenues of $4,824.1M and self-storage cost of operations of $1,177.0M imply a self-storage cost-of-operations intensity of ~24.4% (i.e., gross-like margin ~75.6% before other items such as depreciation/interest).

Industry concentration supports scale-based competition: the Self-Storage Almanac/COLLiers estimates indicate roughly 35.4% combined market share by facilities owned by Publicly listed top operators (Public Companies 22.5% + Other Top Operators 12.9%), implying a materially more consolidated competitive set where large operators like PSA can benefit from operating efficiencies and purchasing/logistics scale relative to fragmented independents.
risks: The operating margin downshift from ~51% (2022–2023) to 46.9% (2024–2025) weakens the evidence that PSA’s scale is currently widening unit-cost advantages versus peers (i.e., less support for a strengthening economies-of-scale moat).

Direct “unit cost vs smaller competitors” metrics (e.g., payroll per square foot, insurance per facility, tenant acquisition cost) and peer-normalized comparisons for Extra Space Storage / CubeSmart are not quantified in the retrieved sources, limiting the ability to prove that smaller operators cannot match PSA’s unit economics.

bear_case: Public Storage disclosed that its decrease in realized annual rent per occupied square foot in 2024 versus 2023 was due to an 11.6% decrease in average rates per square foot charged to new tenants, partially offset by cumulative rate increases to existing long-term tenants.

Public Storage reported meaningful same-store churn (a proxy for tenant turnover) with latest disclosed same-store churn of 18.2% versus 19.6% in the prior-year comparable period, and it continued to operate with customer churn in the high-teens/upper-teens rather than near-zero churn consistent with durable pricing power.

Public Storage’s operating margin fell from 51.9% (2022) to 46.9% (2024 and 2025), indicating margin compression alongside a revenue profile that did not translate into improving unit economics over the last three fiscal years.

Operating margin positive in every year.

Free cash flow positive in every year.

stocks.investment_implication: Realty Income’s narrow moat rests on leasing relationships and pricing power, reinforced by economies of scale. Its moat looks stable, supported by a 105.6% rent recapture rate on properties re-leased in 2024 and an operating margin that rose from 39.1% in 2022 to 45.1% in 2025. However, returns do not confirm a strong moat: approximate ROIC of 2.9% and ROE of 3.5% represent weak financial evidence that capped the rating at 5.9.
stocks.key_strength: Brand Loyalty & Pricing Power: Realty Income re-leased properties at 105.6% of their prior rents in 2024, indicating that its tenant relationships support rental pricing.
stocks.key_risk: Tenant financial distress could weaken rental income and property values, as reflected in $425.8 million of impairment provisions in 2024, up from $87.1 million in 2023.

evidence: Portfolio occupancy was 98.7% at year-end 2024, and Realty Income achieved a 105.6% recapture rate on portfolio units re-leased during 2024 (i.e., re-leased rents exceeded prior rents).
Realty Income reports that it has re-leased over 7,200 properties since 1996 at an average 103.2% recapture rate (recapture rates >100% indicate renewal/pricing power vs prior expirations).

Operating margin increased from 39.1% (2022) to 45.1% (2025), while free cash flow margin remained high (76.7% in 2022, 72.5% in 2023, 67.8% in 2024, 69.5% in 2025), consistent with resilient economics rather than commodity-like pricing.

Reported net margin was volatile but broadly supportive of pricing durability: 26.0% (2022) to 21.4% (2023) to 16.3% (2024) and then 18.4% (2025), implying there was some cost/headwind pressure but not a collapse in underlying operating profitability.

Realty Income’s stated client-relationship strength includes a $770 million sale-leaseback with 7-Eleven (now its top client at 3.5% of annualized rent), described as the sixth such sale-leaseback and growing stronger over nearly a decade of repeat activity.
risks: Return on invested capital is only ~2.9% (latest year), suggesting that even if pricing is resilient, incremental returns may be constrained by capital structure, leverage, and/or reinvestment economics.

Net margin fell materially from 26.0% (2022) to 16.3% (2024), indicating sensitivity to costs (e.g., interest expense, property-level expenses, or transaction costs) that can dilute the economic expression of pricing power.

The business model relies on tenant/lease renewals and recapture rather than directly charging customers 'premium retail rents'; if market leasing spreads or tenant credit conditions deteriorate, recapture rates (and thus effective pricing power) could compress.

evidence: Realty Income’s scale is large but is not a legally/technically protected barrier: as of Dec 31, 2024 it owned or held interests in 15,621 properties leased to 1,565 clients across 89 industries, and it grew to 15,511 properties by Dec 31, 2025—showing scale that entrants can replicate via capital and acquisitions rather than exclusive rights.

The company operates as a REIT with no indication of an exclusive government license or monopoly grant; instead, it states it is required to annually distribute at least 90% of taxable income (excluding net capital gains) in the form of dividends—an industry structure constraint that applies broadly to REITs and does not clearly prevent new REIT entrants.

No company-specific patent/intellectual-property moat is evidenced in the FY2024 Form 10-K PDF search we ran (no matches found for “patent” in the filing), implying limited visible barrier from protectable inventions compared with typical IP-driven business models.

Realty Income’s capital intensity appears largely financing-driven rather than CAPEX-driven: in FY2024 it reported investing $3.9 billion during the year (including investments in properties, development/expansion, and loans) with an initial weighted average cash yield of 7.4%, but this describes business investment, not a disclosed requirement that new entrants must match a specific high fixed CAPEX to compete.

The biggest durable “barrier” visible from the disclosed data is relationship/portfolio execution rather than protection: it had a weighted average remaining lease term of ~9.3 years (excluding tenant extension rights) and $4.97 billion of annualized contractual rent as of Dec 31, 2024, which can make customer-by-customer replacement slower for a newcomer, but it is still achievable through buying portfolios and negotiating new leases.
risks: The analysis may understate barriers because the available documents we searched did not surface a patent portfolio or a detailed, numeric CAPEX-by-line-item “replacement cost” for a new entrant; absent that, the barrier score may be biased downward.

evidence: SBA’s operating margin rose from 37.8% (FY2022) to 41.1% (FY2023), then peaked at 58.6% (FY2024) before moderating to 55.2% (FY2025), indicating sustained cost/lease economics consistent with some pricing power rather than pure commodity pricing.

SBA’s net margin increased from 17.5% (FY2022) to 18.5% (FY2023), then surged to 28.0% (FY2024) and 37.4% (FY2025), supporting that incremental economics (which typically reflect rent levels and escalators net of churn costs) have been favorable over the last ~3 years.

SBA’s free cash flow margin remained very high at 40.7% (FY2022), 48.2% (FY2023), 41.3% (FY2024), and 37.9% (FY2025), which is consistent with durable pricing/renewal economics that convert into cash rather than dissipating through competitive rent resets.

SBA disclosed that it “did experience slightly elevated lease churn” during 2024, attributing it to “some carrier consolidation,” and its materials also reference churn dynamics tied to industry consolidation—evidence that pricing/renewal outcomes are exposed to tenant-driven churn rather than being near-zero.

SBA’s FCC filing characterizes the tower market structure as a shared-infrastructure leasing model with multiple tenants per site and capacity available for additional tenants; this supports that while SBA may have differentiated sites/relationships, tenant choice and re-leasing dynamics can still pressure renewals (i.e., not a frictionless, brand-only pricing power model).
risks: Lease churn is explicitly acknowledged as elevated at times due to carrier consolidation, which can cap pricing power and brand-driven retention (durability risk for the moat on this dimension).

evidence: Scale/asset base: SBA owned and operated 17,464 wireless towers in the United States and its territories as of December 31, 2024, indicating a large incumbent footprint that is difficult for a new entrant to replicate quickly.

Ongoing discretionary + non-discretionary tower CAPEX is substantial: SBA reported total cash capital expenditures of $87.0 million in Q4 2024, consisting of $17.3 million of non-discretionary cash capital expenditures (tower maintenance and general corporate) and $69.7 million of discretionary cash capital expenditures (new tower builds, tower augmentations, acquisitions, and purchasing land and easements).

evidence: SBA Communications’ tenant (carrier) leases for antenna space are generally structured with long initial terms: in the U.S., an initial term of about 5 to 10 years (with renewal periods at the tenant’s option), and internationally an initial term of about 5 to 15 years (with renewal periods at the tenant’s option).

evidence: SBA Communications’ revenue was $2.6B (2022), $2.7B (2023), $2.7B (2024), and $2.8B (2025), indicating modest top-line scale growth (~2.2% CAGR) rather than rapidly widening scale-driven cost advantages.

risks: Economies-of-scale claims are not clearly validated by sustained cost-per-unit improvement: revenue growth is only ~2.2% CAGR (2022–2025) while margins fluctuate (41.1% in 2023 vs 58.6% in 2024 vs 55.2% in 2025), so margin strength may reflect non-scale drivers (pricing, mix, lease structure, one-offs) rather than a consistently widening unit-cost advantage.

SBA operates in a concentrated but competitive market (large neutral hosts plus alternatives). Without explicit evidence of SBA having the lowest unit costs or consistently outbidding peers on tenant pricing/lease renewals, scale may not translate into a structurally unmatchable unit-economics lead over the next decade.

SBA’s forward-looking disclosures quantify meaningful cash site leasing revenue headwinds from consolidation/technology transitions: it expected domestic churn of about $132.0 million to $136.0 million of cash site leasing revenue due to Sprint and EchoStar, implying a material, continuing erosion risk to the moat.
